stem: A company must continuously detect CVEs in 3,000 EC2 instances and ECR images across 40 accounts, rescan automatically when new CVEs are published, prioritize by network exposure, and avoid managing separate scanner agents. Most instances already run the SSM Agent. Which solution fits BEST?

choices.text: Amazon Inspector org-wide via a delegated administrator
AWS Config rules checking installed package versions, with findings aggregated in Security Hub
A third-party scanner AMI in each account, launched weekly by EventBridge to scan instances
GuardDuty Malware Protection

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Inspector continuously scans EC2 (using the SSM Agent, with no separate agent to manage) and ECR images, and automatically rescans when new CVEs appear. Its risk score factors in network reachability, and a delegated administrator enables and views it across the organization.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config package-version rules: Config tracks configuration and isn't a CVE database, so you'd build the vulnerability logic yourself.
• Weekly third-party scanner: not continuous, adds infrastructure, and misses newly published CVEs between runs.
• GuardDuty Malware Protection plus basic scanning: malware isn't CVEs, and basic ECR scanning runs only at push without continuous rescans.

Key takeaway: continuous CVE management for EC2, ECR, and Lambda → Amazon Inspector, org-wide via delegated admin.

stem: A company running a fleet of on-premises VMware VMs needs to implement disaster recovery to AWS with sub-second replication and the ability to fail over entire servers within minutes, without re-architecting the application. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this?

choices.text: AWS Backup
AWS Application Migration Service configured for one-time migration only
AWS DataSync
AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Elastic Disaster Recovery continuously replicates servers at block level to AWS, giving an RPO of seconds and failover within minutes, with non-disruptive drills.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Backup: periodic backups, not continuous replication.
• MGN one-time migration: for migrations, not ongoing DR.
• DataSync: file transfers, not server replication.

Key takeaway: server DR to AWS → Elastic Disaster Recovery.

stem: A company runs its primary application stack in us-east-1 and a fully provisioned standby stack in us-west-2. It wants automatic DNS failover to the standby Region if health checks against the primary fail, without manual DNS changes. What should be configured?

choices.text: Simple routing pointing to the primary Region's endpoint, updated by a runbook during incidents
Route 53 failover routing with health checks on the primary endpoint
Weighted routing split 50/50 between both Regions
A CNAME record that the on-call engineer updates manually to the secondary endpoint

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Failover routing with a health check on the primary answers with the secondary record automatically when the primary is unhealthy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Simple routing with a runbook: manual.
• 50/50 weighted: sends traffic to the standby all the time.
• Manual CNAME: slow.

Key takeaway: automatic DNS DR → failover records + health checks.

stem: A company wants its Amazon Aurora MySQL database's data to be available for near-real-time recovery in a secondary Region with an RPO of a few seconds, and the ability to promote the secondary to a full read/write cluster during a regional disaster. Which Aurora feature should be used?

choices.text: Cross-Region read replicas using MySQL binlog replication plus 15-minute snapshot exports
Aurora Global Database with sub-second lag and fast secondary promotion
Automated backups copied manually to the other Region each day
Aurora Serverless v2 in both Regions with auto-pause enabled

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Aurora Global Database replicates to secondary Regions with typically sub-second lag and supports fast promotion, meeting an RPO of seconds.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Binlog replicas plus snapshots: higher lag and slower recovery.
• Daily manual copies: RPO of a day.
• Serverless auto-pause: not a DR mechanism.

Key takeaway: cross-Region Aurora DR → Global Database.

stem: A firm runs 40 AWS accounts under AWS Organizations and wants identical VPC, logging, and IAM guardrail resources deployed to every current and future account in specific OUs, with updates rolled out centrally. Which approach best meets this?

choices.text: AWS Config rules with auto-remediation in each account
A single CloudFormation stack deployed manually in each account
A Lambda function triggered by account creation that calls the CloudFormation API in each account
CloudFormation StackSets with service-managed permissions targeting the OUs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Service-managed StackSets deploy to target OUs and automatically to new accounts added to them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config remediation: fixes drift, not full baselines.
• Manual stacks: don't scale.
• Custom Lambda on account creation: reinvents StackSets.

Key takeaway: org-wide baselines → StackSets with auto-deployment.

stem: A team's CodePipeline deploys a CloudFormation stack to a production account from a pipeline in a shared tooling account. Deployments must not grant the pipeline broad IAM permissions in production. What should they configure?

choices.text: Grant the pipeline's IAM role AdministratorAccess in the production account
A scoped cross-account role plus a CloudFormation service role in production
Store production account root credentials in Secrets Manager for the pipeline
Move the pipeline into the production account instead of the tooling account

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The pipeline assumes a narrowly scoped cross-account role in production that can only pass a CloudFormation service role, which CloudFormation uses to create resources.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AdministratorAccess: over-privileged.
• Root credentials: never.
• Pipeline in production: couples tooling with production.

Key takeaway: cross-account deployments via scoped roles.

stem: A CodeBuild project's build stage takes 25 minutes because it reinstalls all dependencies from scratch on every build, slowing the CI/CD pipeline significantly. What is the most effective way to reduce build time?

choices.text: Run the build on a persistent EC2 instance
Enable CodeBuild caching (S3 or local) for dependencies
Split the pipeline into more parallel CodePipeline stages
Increase the CodeBuild compute type to the largest available size

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeBuild caching (S3 or local) keeps dependencies between builds, avoiding reinstalling everything each time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Persistent EC2 build server: more operations.
• More parallel stages: doesn't speed dependency installation.
• Bigger compute: faster but still reinstalls.

Key takeaway: repeated dependency installs → caching.

stem: A CloudFormation stack update fails partway through and CloudFormation automatically begins rolling back, but the rollback itself fails, leaving the stack stuck in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED. What is the correct next step?

choices.text: Edit the resource states in the console to match the template, then retry the update
Wait for CloudFormation to retry the failed rollback automatically after a delay
ContinueUpdateRollback, skipping resources that cannot roll back
Delete the stack and manually recreate all of its resources

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ContinueUpdateRollback resumes the rollback and can skip resources that can't be rolled back, returning the stack to a usable state.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Editing states in the console: not possible.
• Automatic retry: doesn't happen.
• Delete and recreate: destructive.

Key takeaway: stuck rollback → ContinueUpdateRollback.

stem: An architect is designing a deployment strategy for a new microservice on ECS Fargate that must shift traffic gradually to a new task set and automatically roll back on CloudWatch alarm triggers, with minimal custom scripting.

choices.text: Deploy a new ECS cluster entirely and manually redirect Route 53 records
CodeDeploy blue/green deployment for ECS with linear traffic shifting and alarm-based rollback
Manually update the ECS service desired count and monitor logs
Use a rolling update deployment configuration in the ECS service directly with no CodeDeploy integration

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeDeploy blue/green for ECS creates a replacement task set, shifts traffic gradually (linear or canary), and rolls back on CloudWatch alarms.

Why the other options are wrong:
• New cluster with manual DNS: slow and manual.
• Manual desired count: no traffic shifting.
• Rolling update without alarms: no automatic rollback.

Key takeaway: gradual ECS releases with rollback → CodeDeploy blue/green.

stem: A company wants to give developers self-service access to provision pre-approved, standardized architectures (e.g., a three-tier web app stack) without giving them direct IAM permissions to create arbitrary resources.

choices.text: Systems Manager Automation documents shared publicly
Grant developers IAM permissions scoped to CloudFormation CreateStack only
AWS Service Catalog with CloudFormation product templates
Give developers read-only console access and have them file tickets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Service Catalog offers approved CloudFormation products that developers can launch themselves, using a launch constraint role instead of broad permissions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public SSM documents: not governed products.
• CreateStack permissions: developers can deploy anything.
• Tickets: not self-service.

Key takeaway: governed self-service → Service Catalog.

stem: A healthcare company must retain copies of critical S3 objects in a separate AWS Region for regulatory business continuity purposes, with replication of new objects happening automatically and asynchronously.

choices.text: S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR)
S3 Same-Region Replication (SRR) only
Manually run the AWS CLI sync command nightly
S3 Transfer Acceleration

explanation:
Why this is correct:
S3 Cross-Region Replication automatically copies objects to a bucket in another Region (with Replication Time Control for SLA-backed timing if needed).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Same-Region Replication: same Region.
• Nightly CLI sync: manual and delayed.
• Transfer Acceleration: speeds uploads.

Key takeaway: copies in another Region → CRR.

stem: Two AWS accounts, Account A (data producer) and Account B (analytics consumer), need Account B's IAM role to read objects from an S3 bucket owned by Account A, following least-privilege principles.

choices.text: Apply only an IAM policy in Account B
A bucket policy in Account A granting the Account B role read access
Copy the data to a bucket in Account B every day through a scheduled export job
Grant Account B's root user full access to Account A through an IAM policy
Make the bucket public and rely on the bucket name being hard to guess

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-account S3 access needs the bucket owner (Account A) to allow the external principal in a bucket policy, in addition to Account B's identity policy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM policy in B only: A hasn't granted access.
• Daily copies: duplication and staleness.
• Root user full access: over-privileged.
• Public bucket: insecure.

Key takeaway: cross-account = resource policy + identity policy.

stem: A company wants RDS database credentials rotated automatically every 30 days without requiring application downtime or manual password updates in application configuration.

choices.text: Keep credentials in an encrypted config file and redeploy the application with new values each month
Rotate the RDS master password manually in the console every 30 days and update the application
Secrets Manager with automatic RDS rotation
Store credentials in Parameter Store as a SecureString parameter with a 30-day expiration policy

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Secrets Manager rotates RDS credentials automatically on a schedule using managed rotation, and applications fetch the current value at runtime, so there's no downtime.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Encrypted config and redeploys: manual.
• Manual console rotation: error-prone.
• Parameter Store SecureString: no built-in rotation.

Key takeaway: automatic DB credential rotation → Secrets Manager.

stem: An Auto Scaling group backs an API whose CPU utilization fluctuates unpredictably. The team wants the group to automatically maintain CPU utilization near a specific target value without manually defining scaling thresholds or step adjustments.

choices.text: Step scaling with multiple CloudWatch alarm thresholds
Target tracking on average CPU utilization
Scheduled scaling actions based on the time of day
Simple scaling policy with a single CloudWatch alarm

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Target tracking keeps average CPU near a target by adding and removing capacity automatically, which suits unpredictable load.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Step scaling: more configuration and tuning.
• Scheduled: the load isn't time-based.
• Simple scaling: slower and coarser.

Key takeaway: hold a metric at a target → target tracking.

stem: An Auto Scaling group terminates instances during scale-in, but the application needs time to gracefully deregister from a service registry and flush in-flight requests before termination completes. What should be configured?

choices.text: A termination lifecycle hook
A longer health check grace period on the group
Instance termination protection on all instances
A longer cooldown period between scaling activities

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A termination lifecycle hook pauses termination so the instance can deregister and drain before it's terminated.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Grace period: about health checks after launch.
• Termination protection: blocks scale-in entirely.
• Cooldown: timing between scaling actions.

Key takeaway: graceful shutdown in ASGs → lifecycle hooks.

stem: Users report intermittent slow response times on a distributed microservices application, but aggregate CloudWatch metrics show no obvious single bottleneck. The team needs to pinpoint which specific service call in a request chain is causing latency.

choices.text: Add more CloudWatch alarms on per-service CPU utilization
Enable VPC Flow Logs and correlate request timestamps across services manually
Enable AWS X-Ray tracing across the services and review segment latencies
Increase CloudWatch metrics to 1-second high resolution

explanation:
Why this is correct:
X-Ray traces individual requests across services and shows segment latencies, revealing where intermittent slowness occurs that averages hide.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More CPU alarms: don't locate slow calls.
• Flow logs and manual correlation: slow and imprecise.
• 1-second metrics: still aggregates.

Key takeaway: find slow hops in distributed systems → tracing.

stem: A high-traffic application uses DynamoDB as its primary data store and needs microsecond read latency for a small set of extremely hot keys accessed millions of times per minute, beyond what DynamoDB alone typically delivers.

choices.text: DynamoDB on-demand capacity mode alone
Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached placed in front of DynamoDB manually with custom cache invalidation logic as the only viable option
Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
DynamoDB Global Tables

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DAX is an in-memory cache for DynamoDB with microsecond reads and minimal code changes (DynamoDB-compatible API).

Why the other options are wrong:
• On-demand: capacity mode, not microsecond reads.
• Memcached with custom logic: more work.
• Global Tables: multi-Region replication.

Key takeaway: microsecond DynamoDB reads → DAX.

stem: A company wants a centralized, policy-driven backup solution across EC2, RDS, DynamoDB, and EFS resources spanning multiple AWS accounts, with backups copied to a separate, logically isolated backup account to protect against ransomware or accidental account compromise. Which approach best meets this?

choices.text: Org-wide AWS Backup policies with cross-account copies to a Vault Lock vault
AWS DataSync jobs that copy nightly exports into another account's S3 bucket
Each service's native snapshot feature configured separately in every account
The default 7-day RDS automated backup retention in each account

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Organization-wide AWS Backup policies centrally define plans for EC2, RDS, DynamoDB, and EFS, with cross-account copies to a vault protected by Vault Lock.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DataSync exports: not backups.
• Per-service snapshots: inconsistent.
• 7-day defaults: insufficient.

Key takeaway: central backup governance → Backup policies.

stem: A European company must ensure that no S3 buckets or RDS instances are ever created outside the eu-west-1 and eu-central-1 Regions across its entire AWS Organization, to satisfy a data residency requirement. The company wants to prevent the action rather than merely detect it afterward. What should they implement?

choices.text: An AWS Config rule that flags and reports resources created in unapproved Regions
An IAM permissions boundary on each user restricting allowed Regions
An OU-level SCP that denies these actions when aws:RequestedRegion is not an approved Region
An EventBridge rule that deletes any resources created in other Regions automatically

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An OU-level SCP denying the actions when aws:RequestedRegion isn't an approved Region prevents creation everywhere in the OU.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config rule: detective.
• Permissions boundaries: per user, easy to miss.
• EventBridge deletion: after the fact.

Key takeaway: prevent Region usage → SCP.

stem: As part of a migration to a multi-account AWS Organizations structure, a company wants its 2,000 employees to sign in once using their existing on-premises Active Directory credentials and access multiple AWS accounts and roles without managing separate IAM users in each account. Which approach should they implement?

choices.text: Configure a separate SAML identity provider trust in each target account manually
IAM Identity Center connected to the existing AD
Amazon Cognito user pools federated independently in each account
IAM users with the same password created in every AWS account

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IAM Identity Center connects to the existing AD, so employees sign in once and receive permission sets across accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SAML per account: unmanageable.
• Cognito: for app users.
• Duplicate IAM users: long-term credentials.

Key takeaway: workforce SSO → Identity Center.

stem: A team migrating a set of containerized batch-processing jobs wants to avoid managing, patching, and scaling EC2 instances for their ECS cluster, and is willing to accept less control over the underlying compute environment in exchange for per-task billing. Which ECS launch type should they choose?

choices.text: AWS Fargate launch type
EC2 launch type using Spot Instances only
EC2 launch type with manual Auto Scaling
ECS Anywhere running on on-premises infrastructure

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fargate runs ECS tasks without managing EC2 instances, patching, or cluster scaling.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EC2 with Spot: still manage instances.
• EC2 with manual scaling: more work.
• ECS Anywhere: your own infrastructure.

Key takeaway: no servers to manage for containers → Fargate.

stem: A company uses AWS CodePipeline with a deploy stage in a different AWS Region than the pipeline itself. The pipeline's artifact S3 bucket is encrypted with a customer managed KMS key. After adding the cross-region deploy stage, the pipeline fails with an access denied error when the deploy stage tries to read the artifact. What is the most likely cause and correct fix?

choices.text: Switch the artifact bucket to SSE-S3, since KMS keys cannot be used across Regions.
Grant the deploy role s3:GetObject only; KMS permissions are not needed for cross-Region artifacts.
Define an artifact store (bucket and KMS key) per Region, with key policies granting decrypt.
Enable S3 Cross-Region Replication on the artifact bucket instead of per-Region artifact stores.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-Region actions need an artifact store per Region. CodePipeline copies artifacts to the Region's bucket, and each Region's KMS key policy must allow the roles that read them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SSE-S3 because KMS can't cross Regions: per-Region keys are the answer.
• GetObject only: SSE-KMS artifacts also need kms:Decrypt.
• CRR instead: CodePipeline manages cross-Region artifacts itself.

Key takeaway: cross-Region pipelines → artifact store (bucket + key) per Region.

stem: A CodeBuild project needs to connect to an RDS MySQL database during integration tests. The security team requires that database credentials be rotated automatically every 30 days without requiring changes to the buildspec each time. Which approach meets this requirement with the least operational overhead?

choices.text: Parameter Store SecureString values rotated every 30 days by a scheduled Lambda function you build.
Secrets Manager with RDS rotation, referenced as a SECRETS_MANAGER env variable.
Plaintext environment variables in buildspec.yml, updated in the repository every 30 days.
A file in a private S3 bucket, downloaded at build time using the project's IAM role.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Secrets Manager with RDS rotation holds the credentials, and the buildspec references it as a secrets-manager environment variable, so nothing is stored in code.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Parameter Store rotated by a Lambda: custom rotation.
• Plaintext in buildspec: exposed in the repo.
• S3 file: weak secret handling.

Key takeaway: build-time DB secrets → Secrets Manager reference.

stem: A DevOps team is migrating source repositories from AWS CodeCommit to GitHub and needs CodePipeline to trigger automatically on every push to the main branch with minimal latency and without storing long-lived GitHub credentials in AWS. Which source action configuration should they use?

choices.text: A CodeStar Connections (GitHub) source action with webhook triggers.
A GitHub source action that polls the repository using CodePipeline's default polling interval.
An EventBridge schedule that calls StartPipelineExecution every 5 minutes.
The GitHub version 1 source action with a personal access token stored as a pipeline parameter.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A CodeConnections (CodeStar Connections) GitHub source action uses a GitHub app installation and webhooks, starting the pipeline on pushes without stored tokens.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Polling: delayed and not the recommended approach.
• Scheduled starts: not event-driven.
• GitHub v1 with a PAT: legacy and stores a token.

Key takeaway: GitHub source → CodeConnections.

stem: An organization needs to store database connection strings used by multiple CodeBuild projects. Some values are static configuration that rarely changes and does not need automatic rotation, while others are credentials that must rotate every 90 days with built-in rotation support. Which combination minimizes cost while meeting these requirements?

choices.text: Everything in Parameter Store advanced tier, with custom Lambda functions rotating all values.
Static values in Parameter Store SecureString; rotating credentials in Secrets Manager.
Everything in Secrets Manager, since it is the only service that encrypts values at rest.
Everything as encrypted environment variables in each CodeBuild project definition.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Static values fit Parameter Store SecureString (low cost), while credentials needing rotation belong in Secrets Manager.

Why the other options are wrong:
• All in advanced Parameter Store with custom rotation: reinvents Secrets Manager.
• All in Secrets Manager: more cost for static values.
• Encrypted env vars per project: duplicated and hard to update.

Key takeaway: match the store to the need for rotation.

stem: A production pipeline must stop after staging until a release manager approves. Approvals must expire if nobody acts within 3 days, the approver must be able to see the staging URL, and only the release-manager group may approve. Which design fits?

choices.text: A Lambda action that sleeps until an approval flag is set in DynamoDB
A CodeBuild step that polls an approval ticket
A Step Functions wait state inserted as a custom action with no timeout
A Manual approval action with SNS and IAM-scoped approvers

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodePipeline's manual approval action pauses the pipeline, notifies through SNS, can include a URL for review, and times out after 7 days if not acted on. Here the 3-day expiry can be enforced by a process or custom automation that rejects the approval, while IAM on codepipeline:PutApprovalResult restricts who can approve.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lambda sleeping: Lambda has a 15-minute limit and isn't a pipeline pause mechanism.
• Step Functions custom action: adds complexity; the built-in approval action already exists.
• CodeBuild polling: wastes build minutes and is fragile.

Key takeaway: human gates in CodePipeline → manual approval action + IAM on PutApprovalResult.

stem: A CodeBuild project that runs integration tests against a private RDS instance was working correctly, but after increasing the number of concurrent builds it began intermittently failing with connection timeouts. The project runs inside a VPC using a dedicated /28 subnet. What is the most likely root cause?

choices.text: Each concurrent build uses an ENI, and the /28 subnet runs out of IP addresses.
The RDS connection limit is reached.
CodeBuild does not support VPC connectivity for concurrent builds of the same project.
The RDS security group does not allow inbound traffic from the CodeBuild security group.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Each VPC-connected CodeBuild build uses an ENI, and a /28 subnet has only 11 usable IPs, so more concurrent builds fail to launch.

Why the other options are wrong:
• RDS connection limit: would cause DB errors, not launch failures.
• No VPC support for concurrency: incorrect.
• SG blocking: would fail single builds too.

Key takeaway: VPC builds consume subnet IPs.

stem: An EC2 in-place CodeDeploy deployment must stop the old app gracefully, back up config before files are copied, set permissions after copying, start the app, and then run a health check that fails the deployment if unhealthy. In which hooks do these scripts belong, in order?

choices.text: ApplicationStop, AfterInstall, BeforeInstall, ValidateService, ApplicationStart
ApplicationStop, BeforeInstall, AfterInstall, ApplicationStart, ValidateService
DownloadBundle, BeforeInstall, Install, AfterInstall, ApplicationStart
BeforeInstall, ApplicationStop, ApplicationStart, AfterInstall, ValidateService

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeDeploy runs ApplicationStop first (using the previous revision's script), then BeforeInstall (pre-copy tasks such as backups), then the Install step copies files, then AfterInstall (permissions and config), ApplicationStart, and finally ValidateService, where a non-zero exit fails the deployment.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Stop after BeforeInstall: the old app should stop before preparation.
• ValidateService before ApplicationStart: you can't validate an app that hasn't started.
• DownloadBundle and Install: reserved steps run by the agent; you can't attach scripts to them.

Key takeaway: remember the order Stop → BeforeInstall → (Install) → AfterInstall → Start → Validate.

stem: A team currently runs Jenkins on self-managed EC2 instances and wants to migrate to a fully managed AWS-native CI/CD solution to reduce operational overhead, while keeping their existing test logic with minimal rework. Which migration approach is most appropriate?

choices.text: Use AWS CodeStar to convert Jenkinsfiles into CodePipeline definitions automatically, without changes.
Translate the Jenkins logic into buildspec commands and CodePipeline stages.
Run the Jenkins controller inside a CodeBuild container and keep everything else unchanged.
Replace every Jenkins pipeline stage with standalone Lambda functions triggered in sequence.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Migrating means translating Jenkins stages into CodePipeline stages and buildspec commands for CodeBuild.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CodeStar conversion: no such conversion.
• Jenkins inside CodeBuild: not managed CI/CD.
• Lambda for every stage: poor fit.

Key takeaway: rebuild the pipeline natively.

stem: After a security team applies a new IAM permissions boundary to all CI/CD service roles, a CodeBuild project that previously deployed CloudFormation stacks starts failing with AccessDenied on cloudformation:CreateStack, even though the CodeBuild service role's attached policy still includes that permission. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The buildspec.yml file must explicitly list every IAM action the build performs.
Permissions boundaries apply only to IAM users, not roles, so this cannot be the cause.
CodeBuild ignores IAM permissions boundaries when it assumes its service role.
The boundary omits cloudformation:CreateStack; effective permissions are the intersection.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Effective permissions are the intersection of the role's policies and its permissions boundary. If the boundary omits cloudformation:CreateStack, the build can't create stacks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• buildspec action lists: not how IAM works.
• Boundaries only for users: they apply to roles too.
• CodeBuild ignores boundaries: it doesn't.

Key takeaway: boundaries cap permissions.

stem: A platform team supports dozens of application teams that each need an identical CI/CD pipeline structure that must be version-controlled, code-reviewed, and easily replicated for new microservices. What approach best achieves this at scale?

choices.text: Export each pipeline's JSON with the CLI and copy it manually for each new team.
Use AWS Config rules to enforce identical stage names after pipelines are created.
A versioned CloudFormation/CDK pipeline template instantiated per team.
Create each pipeline in the console by following a documented runbook.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A versioned CloudFormation or CDK template instantiated per team keeps every pipeline identical and updatable centrally.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Copying JSON: drift.
• Config rules after creation: detection only.
• Console runbook: manual.

Key takeaway: pipelines as code.

stem: A platform stores 15,000 configuration parameters, some 6 KB, read at high rates during deploys. Some parameters must expire automatically after 30 days. Which Parameter Store configuration fits?

choices.text: Standard tier, splitting each 6 KB value across two parameters
Advanced tier with expiration policies
Standard tier, raising the parameter count with a quota increase
Move everything to Secrets Manager, which has no size or rate limits

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Advanced parameters allow a higher total count, values up to 8 KB, and parameter policies such as expiration. Higher throughput is a separate account setting for heavy read loads.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Standard tier with a quota increase: standard values are limited to 4 KB, and there's no parameter policy support.
• Splitting values: fragile and still no expiration policies.
• Secrets Manager: costs more per secret and has its own quotas; it isn't meant for plain configuration.

Key takeaway: large values, policies, or high counts → advanced tier.

stem: A CodePipeline currently uses the default EventBridge-based trigger for its CodeCommit source stage. During a migration, an engineer temporarily reverts the source action to periodic polling. What tradeoff does this introduce?

choices.text: No tradeoff; polling and event-based triggers behave identically in every respect.
Polling is more secure because it does not depend on EventBridge rules.
Polling eliminates cost, while event-based triggers always incur extra charges.
Polling adds start latency and more API calls than event-based triggers.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Polling adds start latency and more API calls compared with event-based triggers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No tradeoff: there is one.
• More secure: not inherently.
• Polling eliminates cost: not true.

Key takeaway: prefer event-driven triggers.

stem: A team wants every merge to main to be releasable, with short-lived branches and no merge hell. It uses GitHub and CodePipeline. Which practice fits BEST?

choices.text: GitFlow with long-lived develop and release branches, each with its own pipeline
Direct commits to main, with tests run weekly by the QA team
Trunk-based development with required CodeBuild PR checks
Feature branches kept open until complete, then merged without CI

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Trunk-based development keeps changes small and merges often into main. Required status checks from CodeBuild on pull requests ensure only passing code merges, and each merge triggers the delivery pipeline.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GitFlow: long-lived branches delay integration and cause merge conflicts.
• Long feature branches without CI: the recipe for merge hell and broken main.
• Weekly tests: defects reach main long before they're found.

Key takeaway: continuous delivery = small, frequent, verified merges to one trunk.

stem: A team wants pull requests opened against their main branch in a GitHub-hosted repository to automatically trigger a CodeBuild project running unit tests, and wants the PR blocked from merging if tests fail, without running a full CodePipeline execution for every PR. Which approach satisfies this?

choices.text: A CodeBuild webhook for PR created/updated events, required as a status check.
Use CodeDeploy's ApplicationStart hook on a test EC2 instance to run the unit tests for each PR.
Trigger CodeBuild builds manually after each pull request is opened by a developer.
Configure CodePipeline to poll for new pull requests and run a full pipeline execution for each one.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A CodeBuild webhook on pull request events runs builds, and a required status check in GitHub blocks merging failing PRs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CodeDeploy hook: deployment, not PR checks.
• Manual builds: unreliable.
• Full pipeline polling: slow and heavy.

Key takeaway: PR validation → webhook + required status check.

stem: A DevOps team must add static application security testing to their pipeline so builds fail automatically when high-severity vulnerabilities are found in application code, before the artifact is published to the artifact repository. How should this be implemented?

choices.text: A build phase that runs SAST and exits non-zero on high-severity findings.
Run the SAST scan only in production after each deployment has completed.
A post-build phase that runs SAST and is reviewed manually after the pipeline completes.
Use Amazon Macie to scan the application source code for security vulnerabilities.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A SAST step in the build that exits non-zero on high-severity findings fails the build automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scan after production: too late.
• Manual review later: not a gate.
• Macie: finds sensitive data, not code vulnerabilities.

Key takeaway: security gates must fail the build.

stem: Before promoting a new microservice version to production, a team needs to run a load test simulating 10,000 concurrent users against staging and automatically fail the pipeline if p99 latency exceeds an SLA. Which pipeline design best achieves this?

choices.text: Rely on CodeDeploy's ValidateService hook during the production deployment to perform the load test.
A staging load-test stage that publishes p99 latency and fails on SLA breach.
A manual step where an engineer runs load tests locally and reports results before approval.
Skip load testing in the pipeline and monitor production traffic after each release instead.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A staging load-test stage that measures p99 latency and fails the pipeline when the SLA is breached prevents slow releases from reaching production.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ValidateService in production: too late and not load testing.
• Local manual tests: inconsistent.
• Monitor production: users are affected.

Key takeaway: performance gates before production.

stem: A CodeDeploy deployment to an Auto Scaling group must confirm that the newly deployed version responds successfully on its /health endpoint before CodeDeploy considers the deployment successful on each instance. Which lifecycle hook should contain this check, and what happens if it fails?

choices.text: Health checks cannot be customized; only the built-in ELB health check can be used.
In ApplicationStop, run before the old version is removed from the instance.
In ValidateService; a non-zero exit fails that instance's deployment.
In BeforeInstall; if it fails, CodeDeploy skips that instance and continues.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ValidateService runs after the application starts, and a non-zero exit fails that instance's deployment.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Can't customize: hooks can.
• ApplicationStop: before install.
• BeforeInstall: before new code exists.

Key takeaway: health validation → ValidateService.

stem: A team wants to add a custom acceptance test step to CodePipeline that isn't supported by any built-in action type, such as calling an internal test orchestration API and waiting for a pass/fail verdict. How can this be integrated?

choices.text: Publish to an SNS topic that triggers the tests asynchronously, without gating the pipeline.
Add a manual approval action and have a person run the acceptance tests instead.
It cannot be done, because CodePipeline supports only its built-in action types.
A Lambda invoke action that reports via PutJobSuccessResult/PutJobFailureResult.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Lambda invoke action runs custom logic and reports the result with PutJobSuccessResult or PutJobFailureResult.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SNS async: no result reported to the pipeline.
• Manual approval: not automated.
• Impossible: Lambda actions exist.

Key takeaway: custom pipeline steps → Lambda invoke action.

stem: A QA team wants to run Selenium-based UI acceptance tests against a freshly deployed staging environment as part of the pipeline, requiring a headless browser and specific driver versions. What is the most appropriate way to run these tests in CodeBuild?

choices.text: Selenium cannot run in CodeBuild.
Use the default managed image and rely on browser software cached between unrelated builds.
Run Selenium locally and paste screenshots into the pipeline's approval action.
A custom CodeBuild image with the browser and driver, running the suite.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A custom CodeBuild image with the browser and WebDriver installed runs Selenium tests headlessly against staging.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Can't run Selenium: it can.
• Cached browsers on the default image: unreliable.
• Local runs with screenshots: not automated.

Key takeaway: special tooling → custom build image.

stem: A pipeline's integration test stage intermittently fails with data conflicts, and investigation shows multiple concurrent pipeline executions from different feature branches all run tests against the same shared RDS test database, causing race conditions. What is the best long-term fix?

choices.text: Increase the RDS instance size so it can handle more concurrent test connections.
Disable integration tests and rely solely on unit tests going forward.
An ephemeral, isolated test database per execution, torn down afterward.
Serialize all pipeline executions so only one runs at a time across the organization.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An isolated, ephemeral database per execution prevents concurrent runs from colliding on shared test data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bigger instance: doesn't isolate data.
• Drop integration tests: loses coverage.
• Serialize all runs: slows delivery.

Key takeaway: isolate test data per run.

stem: A team wants test pass rates and trends in the console for every build, plus code coverage percentages, without custom dashboards. Its tests produce JUnit XML and a Cobertura XML coverage file. Which CodeBuild feature fits?

choices.text: X-Ray traces emitted from the test runner
CloudWatch Logs Insights queries over build logs
Build badges shown in the repository README
Report groups for test and coverage reports

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeBuild report groups read test result files (such as JUnit XML) and code coverage files (such as Cobertura or JaCoCo), and show trends across builds in the console when configured in the buildspec reports section.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Logs Insights: you'd parse text and build dashboards yourself.
• Build badges: show only pass or fail status.
• X-Ray: traces requests, not test results.

Key takeaway: test results and coverage in CodeBuild → report groups.

stem: A team is deciding whether to run unit tests within the same CodeBuild project's build phase (before the artifact is fully packaged) or as a separate CodePipeline stage after the build stage produces artifacts. What is the key tradeoff?

choices.text: Running tests before packaging an artifact is technically impossible in CodeBuild.
Unit tests must always run after deployment to a live environment, so neither option is valid.
In-build tests fail fast; a separate stage isolates concerns but adds latency.
There is no meaningful difference, since stages and phases behave identically.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Running unit tests in the build phase fails fast before packaging. A separate test stage isolates concerns but adds pipeline time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Impossible before packaging: it's common.
• Only after deployment: unit tests don't need a live environment.
• No difference: they differ.

Key takeaway: test placement trades speed for separation.

stem: A company uses a third-party SaaS security scanning service that requires submitting a build artifact, then polling for a scan result that can take up to 20 minutes. Which pipeline design handles this long-running asynchronous external call most robustly?

choices.text: A Lambda action that submits the scan and immediately reports success without waiting for the result.
Submit the scan and report job success or failure only when the real verdict arrives.
Skip automation and have a security engineer check the SaaS dashboard after each deployment.
A CodeBuild phase that submits the scan and sleeps in a polling loop for up to 20 minutes.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The custom action should submit the scan, then report success or failure only when the real verdict is available (for example, via continuation tokens or callbacks).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Report success immediately: unsafe.
• Manual dashboard check: not automated.
• CodeBuild sleep loop: wastes build minutes.

Key takeaway: async external checks → report the real result.

stem: After each production deployment, the team wants synthetic checkout transactions every 5 minutes from outside the VPC, failing and rolling back the deployment if latency exceeds 2 seconds. Which design fits?

choices.text: An ALB health check path with a 2-second timeout
X-Ray sampling rules on the checkout service
A CodeBuild project scheduled every 5 minutes running curl
A Synthetics canary alarm on the deployment group

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudWatch Synthetics canaries run scripted user flows on a schedule and publish metrics. An alarm on canary latency or failures can be attached to the CodeDeploy deployment group for automatic rollback.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ALB health checks: test a single endpoint from inside, not a full transaction.
• CodeBuild cron: rebuilds what canaries provide, with no native rollback link.
• X-Ray: observes real requests; it doesn't generate synthetic transactions.

Key takeaway: synthetic user journeys → Synthetics canaries; tie their alarms to rollback.

stem: A team wants pull requests in their CodeCommit-based workflow to automatically receive code quality and security recommendations, with the ability to block merges when critical issues are found. How should this be integrated?

choices.text: Copy the code manually into the CodeGuru console before every pull request.
CodeGuru Reviewer supports only GitHub repositories, so this cannot be done with CodeCommit.
Use CodeGuru Profiler to analyze pull request code changes for security issues.
Associate the repo with CodeGuru Reviewer and fail builds on open critical findings.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Associating the repository with CodeGuru Reviewer adds PR recommendations, and a build check can fail on open critical findings.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual copy: not automated.
• GitHub only: CodeCommit is supported.
• CodeGuru Profiler: runtime performance.

Key takeaway: PR code review automation → CodeGuru Reviewer.

stem: A pipeline deploys to dev, staging, and production environments requiring different test depths: dev runs only unit tests; staging runs unit, integration, and load tests; production should proceed only if staging's tests and a security scan passed. How should the pipeline be structured to enforce this?

choices.text: Run all test types once at the start of the pipeline and treat the result as valid for every environment.
Deploy to all three environments in parallel and roll back any environment that later fails.
Sequential per-environment stages, each with its required tests.
Use one environment for dev, staging, and production, separated only by feature flags.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Sequential stages per environment, each running its required test depth, promote only builds that pass each gate.

Why the other options are wrong:
• All tests at start: environments differ.
• Parallel deploy: skips gating.
• One environment: no isolation.

Key takeaway: progressive promotion with gates.

stem: A company wants to use approved internal versions of npm and Maven packages while still allowing developers to pull from the public npmjs and Maven Central registries when an internal version isn't yet available, all through a single centrally managed endpoint. Which AWS CodeArtifact configuration achieves this?

choices.text: CodeArtifact cannot connect to public registries, so a VPN link to npmjs.com is required.
Use S3 buckets directly as the package registry instead of CodeArtifact.
One repository with internal upstreams plus an external connection to public registries.
Separate, unconnected repositories for internal and public packages, chosen manually by developers.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A CodeArtifact repository with an internal upstream and an external connection to public registries serves approved internal packages and proxies public ones.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Can't connect public: it can.
• S3 as registry: loses package manager features.
• Separate unconnected repositories: confusing for developers.

Key takeaway: internal + public packages → upstreams and external connections.

stem: A security team wants continuous vulnerability scanning of container images in Amazon ECR that keeps rescanning images as new CVE data becomes available, not just a one-time scan at push. Which ECR scanning configuration should they enable?

choices.text: Basic scanning, which scans each image once at push time.
Enhanced scanning with Amazon Inspector (continuous rescans).
Re-push each image daily to trigger a fresh basic scan.
Amazon Macie scanning of the repository images.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ECR enhanced scanning with Inspector continuously rescans images when new CVEs are published.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Basic scanning: only at push.
• Re-pushing daily: hacky.
• Macie: not vulnerabilities.

Key takeaway: continuous image scanning → enhanced scanning.

stem: A teammate overwrote the prod tag in ECR, and a deployment pulled the wrong image. The team wants to prevent tag overwrites and deploy an exact image that can't change later. What should it do?

choices.text: Enable tag immutability and deploy by digest
Enable ECR enhanced scanning on the repository
Require that all pushes go through one CodeBuild project
Add a lifecycle policy that deletes untagged images

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Tag immutability prevents pushing a new image under an existing tag. Referencing images by digest (sha256) guarantees the exact image content that was tested.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scanning: finds vulnerabilities; doesn't prevent overwrites.
• Lifecycle policy: cleans up images; doesn't protect tags.
• One CodeBuild project: a process control that can still overwrite tags.

Key takeaway: immutable tags + digests = reproducible deployments.

stem: A CodePipeline's S3 artifact bucket has grown to several terabytes because artifacts from every execution over the past two years are retained, increasing storage cost with no compliance requirement to keep them that long. How can costs be reduced while retaining recent artifacts needed for troubleshooting?

choices.text: Move all pipeline artifacts to Amazon EFS instead of S3.
Delete and recreate the bucket, discarding all artifact history at once.
Disable artifact storage so CodePipeline stops producing S3 objects.
An S3 Lifecycle policy to transition and expire old artifacts.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An S3 lifecycle policy transitions and expires old artifacts automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EFS: more expensive.
• Delete and recreate the bucket: loses recent artifacts.
• Disabling artifacts: breaks pipelines.

Key takeaway: artifact growth → lifecycle rules.

stem: A company needs monthly golden AMIs with the latest patches and CIS hardening, automated tests before release, and distribution to 3 Regions and 20 accounts. Launch templates must pick up the new AMI automatically. Which solution fits?

choices.text: An Image Builder pipeline with tests and distribution
A Systems Manager Maintenance Window that patches running instances
An ECR lifecycle policy that rebuilds AMIs monthly
A CodeBuild job calling CreateImage and CopyImage on a schedule

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EC2 Image Builder pipelines build, harden, test, and distribute images across Regions and accounts on a schedule, and distribution settings can update launch templates with the new AMI.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CodeBuild scripts: reinvent testing, distribution, and sharing.
• ECR: stores container images, not AMIs.
• Patching running instances: mutable updates, not golden images.

Key takeaway: golden images at scale → EC2 Image Builder.

stem: A team's Lambda function requires several large ML libraries, pushing the deployment package size close to the zipped package limit. They want a packaging approach supporting significantly larger dependencies that integrates with their existing container-based CI/CD tooling. What should they do?

choices.text: Split the function into many smaller functions to stay under the zip limit.
Keep the .zip package and request a Support increase to the package size limit.
Package the function as a container image in ECR (up to 10 GB).
Move to AWS Batch, since Lambda cannot run ML libraries with any packaging.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Container images in ECR support up to 10 GB, fitting large ML libraries.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Split into many functions: complexity.
• Support increase: the zip limit isn't raised this way.
• Batch only: Lambda can run ML libraries via images.

Key takeaway: large Lambda dependencies → container image.

stem: A central platform team manages a CodeArtifact domain and repository that must be consumed by CodeBuild projects in dozens of separate accounts within an AWS Organization, without duplicating the repository or granting account-level admin access. What is the recommended way to enable this?

choices.text: Grant each consuming account's CodeBuild role AdministratorAccess in the platform account.
Resource policies on the domain/repository granting the needed read actions.
Copy the repository contents to an S3 bucket in each consuming account.
CodeArtifact cannot be shared across accounts, so each account needs its own repository.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeArtifact domain and repository resource policies grant other accounts the read actions they need.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AdministratorAccess: over-privileged.
• Copies to S3: duplication.
• Can't share: it can.

Key takeaway: cross-account package access → resource policies.

stem: An application deploys containers to ECS clusters in both us-east-1 and eu-west-1, and the team wants images pushed to ECR in us-east-1 to automatically become available in eu-west-1 without a manual push step, minimizing pull latency for eu-west-1 clusters. What ECR feature should they configure?

choices.text: S3 Cross-Region Replication
None; ECR does not support any form of cross-Region image replication
ECR private registry cross-Region replication
A script that pulls and pushes images between Regions after every deployment

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ECR private registry replication copies images to other Regions automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 CRR: not for ECR.
• ECR can't replicate: it can.
• Scripts: manual.

Key takeaway: multi-Region images → ECR replication.

stem: A monorepo contains both a containerized backend service and a Lambda-based event processor, and a single CodeBuild project builds both on each commit. What is an appropriate buildspec design to publish both artifact types correctly?

choices.text: It is not possible for a single CodeBuild project to produce more than one artifact type.
Split into two repositories, since a project can reference only one artifact type.
Phases that push the image to ECR and package the Lambda zip in one build.
Use CodeDeploy to build and push the image.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
One CodeBuild project can run commands that build and push an image to ECR and package a Lambda zip, with secondary artifacts if needed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only one output: projects can produce several.
• Split repos: unnecessary.
• CodeDeploy builds images: it doesn't.

Key takeaway: one build can produce multiple artifacts.

stem: A regulated company must produce AMIs that comply with DISA STIG hardening benchmarks, with automated validation that hardening was applied correctly before an AMI is used, and this process must repeat whenever the base AMI is patched. Which approach best satisfies this using AWS-native tooling?

choices.text: Use AWS Config rules to harden instances after they are launched from the AMIs.
Harden one AMI manually and reuse it indefinitely across all workloads.
Image Builder with STIG hardening and test components, run on a schedule.
Use Amazon Inspector to modify AMI configurations to meet STIG requirements.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Image Builder with STIG hardening and test components builds and validates compliant AMIs on a schedule.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config after launch: detection, not hardened images.
• One manual AMI forever: goes stale.
• Inspector modifies AMIs: it doesn't.

Key takeaway: compliant golden AMIs → Image Builder with STIG components.

stem: Developers report that npm install commands in CodeBuild suddenly fail to resolve certain public packages that previously worked, after the platform team added a new internal CodeArtifact repository as an additional upstream ahead of the existing public npm upstream in the dependency chain. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: CodeBuild has a hardcoded allowlist of registries that excludes CodeArtifact.
npm is not supported by CodeArtifact; only pip and Maven are supported.
A repository can have only one upstream, so adding another disabled the first.
The new upstream is first in the chain but not linked through to the public registry.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
If a new upstream is searched first but isn't itself connected to the public registry, resolution can fail. Ensure the chain links to the repository with the external connection.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hardcoded allowlist: not true.
• npm unsupported: it is supported.
• One upstream only: repositories can have several.

Key takeaway: check upstream order and connectivity.

stem: An ECR repository is accumulating a large number of untagged images left behind from a CI process that overwrites tags on every build, consuming storage that is never cleaned up. What is the most appropriate fix?

choices.text: Delete untagged images manually from the ECR console every week.
Enable enhanced scanning, which removes untagged images automatically.
Enable tag immutability, which deletes old untagged images automatically.
A lifecycle policy rule that expires untagged images.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An ECR lifecycle policy rule expires untagged images automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual deletion: toil.
• Enhanced scanning: doesn't delete.
• Tag immutability: prevents overwrites; doesn't clean up.

Key takeaway: image cleanup → lifecycle policies.

stem: A pipeline in Account A builds container images and pushes them to a shared ECR repository, and Account B's ECS service must pull those images. The images must be encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key controlled by Account A, and Account B must be able to decrypt only what is necessary to pull the image, following least privilege. What should be configured?

choices.text: Account A's CMK with key policy and repository policy granting Account B pull and decrypt.
Give Account B full administrative permissions on the key so it can manage the key itself.
Copy the KMS key into Account B so each account holds an independent copy of the material.
Disable repository encryption, since cross-account KMS access is not supported for ECR.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With a customer managed key, the key policy must allow Account B, and the repository policy must allow B to pull.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Admin on the key: over-privileged.
• Copy the key: keys can't be copied.
• Disable encryption: unnecessary.

Key takeaway: cross-account encrypted ECR → key policy + repository policy.

stem: An ASG behind an ALB needs zero-downtime releases, a new fleet for each release, validation before traffic shifts, and instant rollback. Which CodeDeploy approach fits?

choices.text: In-place with OneAtATime on the existing fleet
Blue/green with a replacement Auto Scaling group
A launch template update followed by manual instance termination
In-place with AllAtOnce and a quick rollback script

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeDeploy blue/green for EC2 copies the ASG, deploys and validates on the new instances, shifts ALB traffic, and can keep the old fleet for a set time so rollback just means rerouting.

Why the other options are wrong:
• OneAtATime: slow and modifies existing instances, so rollback means redeploying.
• AllAtOnce: causes downtime.
• Manual termination: no automated validation or rollback.

Key takeaway: new fleet + traffic switch + keep the old fleet = blue/green.

stem: A team deploying an ECS service must choose between an ECS native rolling update and a CodeDeploy-managed blue/green deployment. They require shifting a small percentage of production traffic to the new task set, monitoring CloudWatch alarms, and automatically rolling back before most users are affected. Which approach meets this, and why is the alternative insufficient?

choices.text: CodeDeploy blue/green, which offers canary/linear shifting and alarm rollback.
Rolling updates, because they support traffic-shifting percentages while blue/green does not.
Either one, since both are functionally identical for traffic shifting and rollback.
ECS rolling updates, which shift traffic gradually with alarm-based rollback.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeDeploy blue/green for ECS supports canary and linear traffic shifting with alarm-based rollback.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rolling updates shift percentages: they don't.
• Identical: they differ.
• Rolling with alarm rollback shifting traffic: not the same capability.

Key takeaway: traffic shifting for ECS → CodeDeploy blue/green.

stem: A team wants to shift 10% of production traffic to a new Lambda function version, monitor error rates for 10 minutes, and then automatically shift the remaining 90% if no CloudWatch alarm fires, using an alias for the production endpoint. Which CodeDeploy deployment configuration fits this?

choices.text: CodeDeployDefault.LambdaCanary10Percent10Minutes
CodeDeployDefault.LambdaAllAtOnce with alarms
A linear configuration shifting equal increments every minute
None; Lambda supports only full cutover between versions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
LambdaCanary10Percent10Minutes shifts 10% first, waits 10 minutes, then shifts the rest.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AllAtOnce: no gradual shift.
• Linear: equal steps each interval.
• Lambda full cutover only: false.

Key takeaway: 10% then all after waiting → canary.

stem: A team running workloads on Amazon EKS wants to implement blue/green and canary deployment strategies similar to what CodeDeploy provides natively for ECS and Lambda, but CodeDeploy does not natively manage EKS deployments. What is an appropriate way to implement these strategies within their CI/CD pipeline?

choices.text: Argo Rollouts or Flagger, driven from the pipeline, for metric-based rollouts.
EKS supports only rolling updates, with no possibility of canary or blue/green.
Use CodeDeploy's ECS blue/green deployment type, which also manages EKS.
Edit Deployment replica counts manually to simulate blue/green deployments.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Argo Rollouts or Flagger provide blue/green and canary strategies with metric-based promotion for Kubernetes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rolling only: not true with these tools.
• CodeDeploy ECS for EKS: not supported.
• Manual replica edits: error-prone.

Key takeaway: progressive delivery on EKS → Argo Rollouts / Flagger.

stem: Two incidents came from servers that drifted after SSH hotfixes, and one rollback took hours because the previous state was unknown. Which deployment pattern prevents both problems?

choices.text: Mutable deployments with a configuration management agent
Immutable deployments from versioned artifacts
Mutable deployments with SSH changes logged in a wiki
Snapshots before every change

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Immutable deployments never change running servers. Each release is a new versioned image or artifact on new instances, so every server matches a known version, and rollback means redeploying the previous version.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config management agents: reduce drift but still mutate servers.
• Logged SSH changes: documentation doesn't prevent drift.
• Snapshots: help restores, but in-place changes still drift.

Key takeaway: immutable = known state and fast rollback.

stem: A stateful application stores session data on an instance-attached EBS volume that is not shared or replicated, and the team is considering moving from CodeDeploy in-place deployments to blue/green to reduce deployment risk. What key tradeoff must they address first?

choices.text: New instances get fresh volumes; externalize session state before adopting blue/green.
Blue/green migrates EBS data to new instances automatically, so there is no tradeoff at all.
Blue/green cannot be used with any application that uses EBS volumes.
In-place deployments also lose local EBS data every time, so there is no difference.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Blue/green creates new instances with fresh volumes, so local session data is lost. Externalize session state first.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Automatic EBS migration: doesn't happen.
• Can't use EBS: it can for stateless apps.
• In-place loses data: it doesn't.

Key takeaway: externalize state before immutable deployments.

stem: A static website hosted in S3 and served through CloudFront needs a blue/green deployment approach so a new version can be fully validated before any production users see it, with an instant, low-risk cutover and easy rollback. Which architecture best supports this?

choices.text: Deploy to a separate bucket, validate, then switch the CloudFront origin.
Use CodeDeploy's ValidateService hook against the bucket.
Blue/green concepts do not apply to static content served from S3 and CloudFront.
Overwrite objects in the bucket and invalidate the CloudFront cache, with no separate validation.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Deploy the new version to a separate bucket (or prefix), validate it, then switch the CloudFront origin, keeping the old one for rollback.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CodeDeploy hook: not for S3.
• Doesn't apply: it does.
• Overwrite and invalidate: no clean rollback.

Key takeaway: static blue/green → switch origins.

stem: An application deployed via CodeDeploy blue/green to EC2 instances stores uploaded user files on an Amazon EFS file system mounted by all instances. When the new green fleet is provisioned, what is the correct expectation regarding this shared storage, and what should the team verify?

choices.text: EFS cannot be used with Auto Scaling groups, so uploads must move to EBS first.
Blue/green requires a separate EFS file system for the green fleet, duplicating all data.
EFS is shared, so the green fleet can mount it; verify mounts and NFS rules.
EFS data must be copied to the new fleet manually.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EFS is a shared file system, so the green fleet can mount the same file system. Verify mount configuration and NFS security group rules for new instances.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EFS incompatible with ASGs: it isn't.
• Separate EFS per fleet: duplicates data.
• Manual copies: unnecessary.

Key takeaway: shared state lives outside instances.

stem: A team is choosing a CodeDeploy deployment configuration for an in-place EC2 deployment behind an ELB with 20 instances, wanting to balance deployment speed against the risk of taking too much capacity offline at once, without writing a custom configuration. How do the built-in extremes compare, and what fills the middle ground?

choices.text: Deployment configurations apply only to Lambda and ECS, not to EC2 in-place deployments.
OneAtATime deploys to all 20 instances concurrently, despite its name.
AllAtOnce is fastest but drops capacity; OneAtATime is safest but slowest.
AllAtOnce is the safest option because it minimizes the deployment window.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AllAtOnce is fastest but removes all capacity during deployment. OneAtATime is safest but slowest.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Configs only for Lambda/ECS: EC2 supports them.
• OneAtATime is concurrent: it isn't.
• AllAtOnce safest: it isn't.

Key takeaway: deployment speed vs. capacity risk.

stem: A CodeDeploy deployment to an EC2 fleet fails partway through because a lifecycle hook script returns a non-zero exit code on several instances, but the deployment group has no automatic rollback configured and no CloudWatch alarms attached. What happens to the fleet after this failure?

choices.text: The failure is ignored, and CodeDeploy marks the deployment as Succeeded.
CodeDeploy terminates all instances in the fleet after any lifecycle hook failure.
CodeDeploy always rolls back all instances, since rollback is enabled by default.
It is marked Failed and the fleet is left mixed until manually redeployed.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A failed hook marks the deployment Failed. Without automatic rollback configured, instances are left with mixed versions until redeployed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Failure ignored: not true.
• Terminates instances: not true.
• Rollback by default: must be enabled.

Key takeaway: configure automatic rollback.

stem: A team is adopting blue/green deployments for an application backed by a single shared RDS database, where the new application version requires a backward-incompatible schema change. What is the primary challenge, and what is the recommended mitigation?

choices.text: Delete and recreate the database during every blue/green deployment to avoid the issue.
This challenge applies only to Lambda deployments, not EC2 or ECS sharing an RDS instance.
There is no challenge, since blue/green provisions a migrated copy of the database.
Both versions share the database during the shift; use expand-and-contract.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
During traffic shifting, both versions use the same database. Expand-and-contract schema changes keep the schema compatible with both.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Recreate the DB: data loss.
• Lambda-only issue: applies to all.
• Migrated copy: blue/green doesn't copy databases.

Key takeaway: shared databases need backward-compatible changes.

stem: A team must choose between a linear and a canary traffic-shifting configuration for a Lambda deployment using CodeDeploy and wants to understand the fundamental difference between the two shifting patterns. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Linear and canary are two names for the same behavior in CodeDeploy.
Canary shifts once then the rest; linear shifts equal steps at intervals.
Linear requires manual approval between each increment, while canary does not.
Canary always completes the shift in exactly two steps of 50% each.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Canary shifts a portion once, then the rest after a wait. Linear shifts equal increments at regular intervals.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Same behavior: different.
• Manual approval between steps: not required.
• Always 50/50: not true.

Key takeaway: canary = two steps; linear = many equal steps.

stem: A CodeDeploy blue/green deployment for an ECS service repeatedly fails because the new task set is marked unhealthy and rolled back before the application finishes a lengthy startup process involving loading large in-memory caches, even though it eventually becomes healthy about 3 minutes after starting. What change is most likely to resolve this?

choices.text: Reduce the number of tasks in the new task set so they start faster.
Disable health checks on the target group.
Switch to an ECS rolling update, which has no health check requirements.
Lengthen the grace period and tune target group health checks.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
New tasks marked unhealthy during startup need a longer health check grace period and suitable target group health settings.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Fewer tasks: doesn't fix health.
• Disable health checks: unsafe.
• Rolling updates: still need health.

Key takeaway: slow starts → grace period and health tuning.

stem: A SAM template deployment fails with 'Transform AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31 failed'. The team deploys with plain aws cloudformation create-stack. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: It's a CloudFormation transform; add CAPABILITY_AUTO_EXPAND
SAM templates are deployed by the Lambda service and can't be used with CloudFormation
SAM templates must first be compiled to Terraform
The transform runs only in the SAM CLI, so CloudFormation can't process it

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SAM is a CloudFormation transform (macro) that expands resources such as AWS::Serverless::Function into standard resources. Deploying a template with transforms through CloudFormation requires acknowledging CAPABILITY_AUTO_EXPAND (typically with a change set).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lambda deploys it: CloudFormation deploys SAM templates.
• Terraform: unrelated.
• CLI-only: CloudFormation processes the transform server-side.

Key takeaway: SAM = CloudFormation transform; acknowledge auto-expand capability.

stem: A team currently maintains large, repetitive CloudFormation JSON templates for dozens of similar microservice stacks and wants to reduce duplication using loops, conditionals, and typed objects while still being able to inspect the exact resources that will be created before deployment. Which approach best satisfies this requirement?

choices.text: Use nested stacks only, since they remove the need for repeated resource declarations.
Rewrite the templates with CloudFormation macros, the only way to add logic to templates.
Adopt the CDK with reusable constructs, reviewing output with cdk synth.
Migrate to AWS OpsWorks stacks.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The CDK lets you define reusable constructs in code, reducing repetition, and cdk synth shows the generated templates for review.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Nested stacks only: still JSON repetition.
• Macros only: not the only way to add logic.
• OpsWorks: configuration management.

Key takeaway: repetitive templates → CDK constructs.

stem: An engineer discovers that a production CloudFormation stack shows several resources as MODIFIED after running drift detection, including a security group whose inbound rules were changed manually during an incident. The team wants to reconcile the stack to match the current, drifted production configuration without immediately reverting the manual change, while still being able to manage the resource with CloudFormation going forward. What should they do?

choices.text: Run continue-update-rollback.
Update the template to match the drift, then review a change set before executing.
Ignore the drift, since CloudFormation automatically reconciles drifted resources on the next stack update.
Delete and recreate the stack from the original template so all resources return to their defined state.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
If the drifted values should be kept, update the template to match them and review a change set before executing; otherwise the next update may revert or fail.

Why the other options are wrong:
• continue-update-rollback: for stuck rollbacks.
• Ignore: CloudFormation doesn't auto-reconcile drift.
• Delete and recreate: disruptive.

Key takeaway: resolve drift deliberately through the template.

stem: A cloud platform team wants to publish a governed, versioned building block that provisions a standardized VPC, with specific subnet counts, NACLs, and flow log configuration, so that other teams can embed it directly inside their own CloudFormation templates as a single resource type, with updates rolled out by publishing a new version. Which CloudFormation feature is purpose-built for this?

choices.text: A nested stack template referenced by a hardcoded S3 URL
CloudFormation StackSets deployed to each account
A CloudFormation module in the registry
A Service Catalog product with a launch constraint

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFormation modules in the registry package a governed, versioned building block that templates can reuse.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hardcoded nested stack URL: weak versioning.
• StackSets: deployment, not a reusable building block.
• Service Catalog product: for launching products, not composing within templates.

Key takeaway: reusable template components → modules.

stem: A mobile backend team wants to roll out a new pricing algorithm to a Lambda-based API gradually, monitor CloudWatch alarms during the rollout, and automatically halt and roll back the configuration change if error rates spike, without redeploying application code. Which AWS service is designed for this use case?

choices.text: Secrets Manager automatic rotation of the pricing value
Parameter Store standard parameters read at invocation
AppConfig with a gradual deployment strategy and alarm monitor
CloudFormation change sets with manual approval for each change

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AppConfig deploys configuration or feature flags gradually, monitors alarms, and rolls back automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Secrets Manager rotation: secrets.
• Parameter Store: no gradual rollout.
• Change sets: infrastructure.

Key takeaway: gradual config rollout → AppConfig.

stem: A DevOps team is deciding where to store two categories of configuration data used by their CI/CD pipeline: database credentials that must rotate automatically every 30 days, and non-sensitive environment names and feature toggles referenced by dozens of CloudFormation templates. Which approach is most cost-effective and appropriate?

choices.text: Credentials in Secrets Manager with rotation; other config in Parameter Store standard.
Both in Parameter Store advanced parameters with a custom Lambda rotation schedule.
Both in Secrets Manager, the only service supported by CloudFormation dynamic references.
Credentials in Parameter Store with manual Lambda rotation; toggles in Secrets Manager.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Credentials go in Secrets Manager with rotation, and other configuration in Parameter Store.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Custom rotation in Parameter Store: reinvents Secrets Manager.
• Only Secrets Manager supported: both have dynamic references.
• Credentials in Parameter Store: no managed rotation.

Key takeaway: secrets vs. config: different stores.

stem: A legacy OpsWorks Stacks layer must install a monitoring agent automatically on every new instance as soon as it boots, and again after any instance is replaced. Which lifecycle event should run the recipe?

choices.text: Configure
Setup
Deploy
Shutdown

explanation:
Why this is correct:
OpsWorks runs Setup recipes when an instance finishes booting, which suits installing agents and base packages on every new instance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Deploy: runs when an app is deployed.
• Configure: runs on all instances when an instance enters or leaves the online state, meant for updating configuration such as peer lists.
• Shutdown: runs before an instance stops.

Key takeaway: boot-time installs → Setup; topology changes → Configure. (For new work, prefer Systems Manager.)

stem: A team is deciding between CloudFormation nested stacks and cross-stack references, using Export and Fn::ImportValue, to share a VPC's subnet IDs with multiple independently owned application stacks. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two approaches?

choices.text: Cross-stack references let the exporting stack change freely while imports exist; nested stacks block parent updates.
Cross-stack references use AWS::CloudFormation::Stack, while nested stacks use Fn::ImportValue.
Nested stacks share one owner's lifecycle; exports serve independent stacks but block changing used outputs.
They are functionally identical; the only difference is how template files are organized.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
