The cluster must use the EC2 launch type, since Fargate cannot use target tracking.
The service is already at the scalable target's maximum task count.
ECS services can scale only on memory metrics, not CPU utilization.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
If the service is already at the scalable target's maximum capacity, target tracking can't add tasks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Logs subscription required: no.
• Fargate can't use target tracking: it can.
• Memory only: CPU works.

Key takeaway: check min/max bounds when scaling stalls.

stem: A CloudWatch alarm monitors disk space on a fleet of EC2 instances and needs to automatically run a cleanup script on the affected instance when it enters ALARM state, in addition to notifying the on-call engineer. Which design achieves automated remediation and notification together?

choices.text: SNS to the on-call engineer and to a Lambda that runs the cleanup via Run Command.
Trigger an Auto Scaling scheduled action that reboots the instance nightly.
Write the alarm to a log group and rely on a metric filter to run the cleanup script.
Invoke AWS Config directly, which runs the cleanup script as a remediation action.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The alarm publishes to SNS, which notifies on-call and invokes a Lambda function that runs the cleanup on the instance through SSM Run Command.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Nightly reboot: not targeted.
• Metric filter to run scripts: not how it works.
• Config remediation from an alarm: not the mechanism here.

Key takeaway: alarm → SNS → Lambda → SSM for automated fixes.

stem: A company wants any EC2 instance found by an AWS Config rule to be missing the required CloudWatch agent installation to be automatically remediated by installing and starting the agent via Systems Manager, without manual operator action. Which configuration accomplishes this?

choices.text: Config remediation with an SSM Automation document to install and start the agent.
Enable Systems Manager Inventory.
Alarm on the rule's compliance metric and email the team to install the agent manually.
Use AWS Config to install software on non-compliant resources directly, without SSM.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Config remediation action running an SSM Automation document installs and starts the CloudWatch agent on noncompliant instances.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Inventory: reports, doesn't install.
• Email: manual.
• Config installs software: via SSM remediation, not directly.

Key takeaway: auto-fix instance configuration → Config + SSM Automation.

stem: An Application Load Balancer is marking healthy EC2 targets as unhealthy and removing them from rotation during brief periods of high CPU load, even though the application recovers within a few seconds and would have served the next request successfully. Users experience intermittent 503 errors during these periods. What should be adjusted to reduce unnecessary target deregistration during brief transient slowness?

choices.text: Raise UnhealthyThreshold and/or the interval and timeout.
Remove the health check so targets are never marked unhealthy.
Switch to TCP health checks, which ignore application slowness.
Shorten the health check interval.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Brief slowness shouldn't fail targets. Raising the unhealthy threshold and/or the interval and timeout tolerates transient spikes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove health checks: unsafe.
• TCP checks: less meaningful.
• Shorter interval: more flapping.

Key takeaway: tune health checks to avoid flapping.

stem: A team currently uses EventBridge rules with cron expressions to trigger Lambda functions on fixed schedules, but as the number of scheduled jobs grows into the thousands across accounts, they hit default EventBridge rule quotas and want a purpose-built scheduling service with higher scalability, at-least-once delivery guarantees, and native support for time zones and one-time schedules. Which service should they migrate to?

choices.text: Amazon EventBridge Scheduler
AWS Config scheduled rules for high-scale job scheduling
Amazon Inspector scheduled scans invoking Lambda functions
CloudWatch Logs scheduled queries that invoke Lambda

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EventBridge Scheduler is built for large numbers of schedules, with time zones, one-time schedules, and flexible windows.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config scheduled rules: compliance.
• Inspector scans: vulnerabilities.
• Logs scheduled queries: not a scheduler for Lambda.

Key takeaway: many schedules → EventBridge Scheduler.

stem: A team is considering enabling automatic remediation on an AWS Config rule that terminates EC2 instances launched with unencrypted EBS volumes. What is the primary risk of enabling fully automatic remediation for this specific rule compared to manual approval-based remediation?

choices.text: Automatic remediation requires the instance to be terminated already, so there is no extra risk.
Config does not support manual remediation approval, so the comparison is invalid.
A misfiring automatic termination can destroy production; manual approval adds a check.
Config does not support automatic remediation for EBS-related rules at all.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Automatic termination can destroy production if the rule misfires. Manual approval adds a safety check at the cost of slower response.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Instance already terminated: false.
• No manual approval support: manual remediation exists.
• No EBS remediation: not the point.

Key takeaway: weigh blast radius before auto-remediating destructively.

stem: A company runs workloads across 20 AWS accounts managed through AWS Organizations. The security team wants a single centralized location to receive AWS Health events (including scheduled maintenance and abuse notifications) from every member account without requiring each account to configure its own forwarding rule from scratch. Which approach meets this requirement with the least ongoing per-account configuration?

choices.text: An EventBridge rule in each member account forwarding aws.health events to an SQS queue in the security account.
A Config aggregator in the management account that collects Health events from members.
Health organizational view plus an EventBridge rule on aws.health to one SNS topic.
Subscribe the security team's email to each account's Personal Health Dashboard RSS feed.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Health organizational view aggregates events across accounts, and an EventBridge rule on aws.health events routes them to the security team.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rules in each account: more setup (though possible).
• Config aggregator: doesn't collect Health events.
• Email per account: fragmented.

Key takeaway: org-wide Health events → organizational view + EventBridge.

stem: A DevOps engineer configured an EventBridge rule to trigger a Lambda function whenever a specific S3 object is deleted, matching CloudTrail's DeleteObject event. The rule works for management events like bucket policy changes but never fires for the object delete calls. What is the most likely cause and fix?

choices.text: The Lambda function's execution role lacks s3:GetObject permission.
CloudTrail delivers events only to CloudWatch Logs, not EventBridge, so the rule never matches.
S3 object-level calls aren't logged by default; enable S3 data events.
EventBridge cannot match S3 API calls, so S3 Event Notifications must be used instead.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
S3 object-level API calls (such as DeleteObject) are CloudTrail data events, not logged by default. Enable S3 data events so EventBridge receives them (or use S3 Event Notifications to EventBridge).

Why the other options are wrong:
• s3:GetObject permission: unrelated to triggering.
• CloudTrail doesn't deliver to EventBridge: it does.
• EventBridge can't match S3 calls: it can with data events.

Key takeaway: object-level events need data event logging.

stem: A security team wants to be alerted in near real time whenever any IAM user or role calls CreateAccessKey, and separately wants AWS to automatically detect unusual spikes in API call volume or error rates without the team having to define specific API names or thresholds to watch. Which combination of services satisfies both requirements?

choices.text: An EventBridge rule on CreateAccessKey plus CloudTrail Insights for anomalies.
AWS Config rules that evaluate IAM resource configurations on a periodic schedule.
One metric filter on the CloudTrail log group counting IAM calls, with a threshold alarm.
GuardDuty findings sent to EventBridge, covering both needs without CloudTrail setup.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An EventBridge rule matching CreateAccessKey gives near-real-time alerts, and CloudTrail Insights detects anomalous call volumes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Periodic Config rules: slow.
• One metric filter: no anomaly baseline.
• GuardDuty alone: different detections.

Key takeaway: specific API alerts → EventBridge; anomalies → Insights.

stem: An incident response pipeline uses an EventBridge rule to invoke a Lambda function directly whenever a GuardDuty finding is published. During a recent incident storm, several findings were dropped because the Lambda function's concurrency limit was reached and EventBridge's retry policy expired before capacity freed up. Which change would most effectively prevent event loss during future bursts while preserving ordering-independent processing?

choices.text: Target an SQS queue and have Lambda poll it with sized batches and concurrency.
Target a Step Functions Express workflow instead, which has no concurrency limits.
Raise Lambda reserved concurrency to a very high value so it is never throttled.
Set the rule's retry attempts to 0 so failed invocations are discarded quickly.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Targeting an SQS queue buffers bursts, and Lambda polls with controlled batch sizes and concurrency, so findings aren't dropped or overwhelm downstream.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Express workflow: still concurrency concerns.
• Huge reserved concurrency: may overload downstream.
• Zero retries: loses events.

Key takeaway: buffer bursts with a queue.

stem: A company's fleet of thousands of edge devices generates security telemetry that must be ingested at a sustained rate of over 50,000 records per second, retained for replay by multiple independent consumer applications (a real-time anomaly detector and a batch archiver), and processed in order per device. Which event source is best suited to this ingestion requirement?

choices.text: A single EventBridge custom bus with two rules targeting each consumer.
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, using the device ID as the partition key.
Amazon SQS FIFO queue, since it guarantees ordering.
Amazon SNS with multiple subscribers for fan-out.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Kinesis Data Streams handles high sustained ingest, preserves order per partition key (device ID), and supports multiple consumers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EventBridge bus: not for sustained high-volume streams.
• SQS FIFO: throughput limits.
• SNS: no ordering or replay.

Key takeaway: high-volume ordered streams → Kinesis.

stem: A DevOps team wants to automate response to high-severity Security Hub findings: automatically isolate the affected EC2 instance's security group, but require a human approval step via email before terminating the instance if isolation does not resolve the issue within 30 minutes. Which service is best suited to orchestrate this multi-step, long-running workflow with a wait-for-callback human approval pattern?

choices.text: Amazon EventBridge Scheduler configured to invoke a Lambda function every 5 minutes to poll for approval.
A single Lambda function with a sleep() call for 30 minutes before checking approval status.
AWS Systems Manager Automation with only automatic remediation steps, no human approval capability.
AWS Step Functions using the waitForTaskToken integration pattern with SNS for the approval notification.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Step Functions with waitForTaskToken can isolate the instance automatically, then pause for a human decision before further actions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scheduler: not event-driven.
• Lambda sleep: 15-minute limit.
• SSM automatic only: no human gate as described.

Key takeaway: automation with human approval → task tokens.

stem: A team currently uses an EventBridge rule with an input transformer to reshape events from an SQS queue before invoking a target, but the transformation logic is error-prone, and they want to add an enrichment step that calls an external API to add context before delivery, plus built-in filtering, all without writing a Lambda function purely for plumbing. Which EventBridge feature is purpose-built for this point-to-point flow?

choices.text: EventBridge Pipes
EventBridge Archive and Replay
EventBridge Schema Registry
A second rule chained to the first rule's target

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EventBridge Pipes connects a source (such as SQS) to a target with optional filtering, enrichment, and transformation, without writing glue code.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Archive and replay: event history.
• Schema Registry: schemas.
• Chained rules: can't read from SQS.

Key takeaway: point-to-point source → target with transform → Pipes.

stem: A company enabled an AWS Organizations CloudTrail trail in the management account and created an EventBridge rule in the management account to detect root user console sign-ins across all accounts, targeting a Lambda function for alerting. During a security drill, a root sign-in occurred in a member account but no alert fired, and the trail is confirmed to be logging correctly across all accounts. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: Organization trails never generate events for member accounts, only for the management account.
Root user activity is never logged by CloudTrail for security reasons.
The rule's event pattern doesn't correctly match Root ConsoleLogin events.
EventBridge rules cannot be created in the management account.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Root console sign-in events have their own source and detail-type (aws.signin, 'AWS Console Sign In via CloudTrail') and are delivered in specific Regions (for example, us-east-1 for global sign-ins). A pattern that doesn't match these misses them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Org trails ignore members: they log members.
• Root activity not logged: it is.
• Management account can't have rules: it can.

Key takeaway: match event patterns to the exact source, type, and Region.

stem: An EventBridge rule invokes a Lambda function asynchronously. The team wants to capture the full event payload plus the function's response for successful invocations for downstream analytics, and separately capture failed invocations after retries are exhausted for reprocessing. Which configuration achieves both without writing custom code inside the function to publish results?

choices.text: Add try/catch logic in the function to publish results to SNS on success and failure.
Lambda destinations for on-success and on-failure.
A dead-letter queue only, since it captures both successful and failed payloads.
Enable X-Ray tracing, which stores successful and failed payloads in S3.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lambda destinations for asynchronous invocations capture the full event plus the result (on success) or error details (on failure) and send them to targets.

Why the other options are wrong:
• try/catch to SNS: custom and incomplete.
• DLQ: failed events only, without results.
• X-Ray: traces, not payload storage.

Key takeaway: async outcomes → destinations.

stem: A central security account has an EventBridge rule intended to receive GuardDuty findings forwarded from ten member accounts via a custom event bus. Findings from nine accounts arrive correctly, but events from the tenth account never appear, even though CloudTrail confirms GuardDuty is generating findings there. What should the engineer check first?

choices.text: Whether the tenth account has enabled AWS Config.
Whether GuardDuty is enabled in the central security account.
The target bus ARN in that account and the bus policy allowing its PutEvents.
Whether the central account's IAM user has AdministratorAccess.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-account forwarding needs the member account's rule to target the correct central bus ARN, and the central bus policy must allow that account to PutEvents.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config enabled: unrelated.
• GuardDuty in central account: unrelated to forwarding.
• Admin IAM user: unrelated.

Key takeaway: cross-account events = correct target + bus policy.

stem: The team wants automatic remediation when AWS announces an issue or scheduled maintenance affecting its own EC2 instances, across 20 accounts. Which design fits?

choices.text: CloudTrail Insights on EC2 API calls
Health organizational view with EventBridge rules
Poll the public service health page every minute
Trusted Advisor checks with weekly email

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The AWS Health API and events are specific to your resources. Organizational view aggregates them, and EventBridge rules on aws.health events can trigger automation such as Lambda or SSM runbooks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public health page: general status, not tied to your resources.
• Trusted Advisor: best-practice checks, not service events.
• CloudTrail Insights: unusual API activity, not AWS service issues.

Key takeaway: account-specific AWS events → Health + EventBridge.

stem: A team needs to run a lightweight remediation Lambda function every 15 minutes to check for and terminate orphaned EC2 instances tagged for cleanup, with no need for multi-step orchestration, retries across multiple services, or workflow state. Which approach introduces the least operational overhead?

choices.text: Set up a Systems Manager Automation runbook triggered by a CloudWatch Events rule with a rate expression.
Build a Step Functions state machine with a 15-minute wait state in a loop, running continuously.
Create an EventBridge Scheduler schedule that invokes the Lambda function directly every 15 minutes.
Create an AWS Config rule with a periodic trigger of 15 minutes that invokes the Lambda function as a remediation action.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EventBridge Scheduler invokes the Lambda function every 15 minutes with no extra infrastructure.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SSM runbook via alarm: indirect.
• Step Functions wait loop: pays for orchestration.
• Config periodic rule: minimum intervals and wrong purpose.

Key takeaway: simple recurring invocation → EventBridge Scheduler.

stem: A compliance team must deploy the same versioned set of 30 AWS Config rules with remediation to 50 accounts, including accounts added later, and report one compliance score per account for that set. Which AWS Config feature fits BEST?

choices.text: An organization conformance pack deployed from the Config delegated administrator
Individual Config rules created in each account by a StackSet, with scores calculated in a spreadsheet
Firewall Manager security group policies applied across the organization
A Config aggregator in the audit account that pushes the rules to member accounts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Conformance packs bundle Config rules and remediation actions into one versioned template. Organization conformance packs deploy that bundle to all member accounts, including new ones, and Config reports a compliance score per conformance pack for each account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Individual rules via StackSets: they deploy, but the rules aren't managed as a package and there's no native per-pack score.
• Aggregators: collect and display data across accounts. They don't deploy rules.
• Firewall Manager security group policies: manage security groups, not arbitrary compliance rule sets.

Key takeaway: deploy a rule bundle org-wide → organization conformance pack; view results centrally → aggregator.

stem: An Auto Scaling group launches new instances that require several post-boot configuration steps, including installing an agent, registering with a monitoring system, and running a validation script, before they should start receiving traffic. The team wants this orchestrated automatically whenever a new instance launches, with the instance remaining pending until the steps succeed. Which design meets this requirement?

choices.text: A Config rule that evaluates the instance after it has already entered InService.
The default health check grace period, which holds instances out of service until ready.
A launch lifecycle hook with EventBridge triggering an SSM runbook, then CompleteLifecycleAction.
User data that runs all steps synchronously, with no lifecycle hook needed.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A launch lifecycle hook holds new instances in Pending:Wait while EventBridge triggers an SSM runbook to configure them, then completes the hook so they enter service ready.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config after InService: too late.
• Grace period: doesn't run configuration.
• Synchronous user data only: no controlled gate or retry.

Key takeaway: gate new instances until ready → launch lifecycle hooks.

stem: A team is deciding how to remediate AWS Config non-compliance findings for unencrypted EBS volumes. Option one uses AWS Config's built-in automatic remediation feature with an AWS-managed SSM Automation document. Option two uses a custom Lambda function triggered by an EventBridge rule matching Config compliance change events. What is a key operational tradeoff favoring option one for this use case?

choices.text: Custom Lambda is always cheaper, because Config charges per remediation while Lambda is free.
Config's built-in remediation cannot use SSM documents and requires Lambda anyway.
Built-in remediation adds retries, rate limits, and audit trail, limited to the SSM document.
The custom Lambda approach provides a compliance audit trail that Config remediation lacks.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Config's built-in remediation with SSM documents provides retries, rate limits, and an audit trail. A custom Lambda offers flexibility but you build those features yourself.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lambda always cheaper: not the point.
• Can't use SSM: it uses SSM documents.
• Lambda gives better audit: Config tracks remediation.

Key takeaway: prefer managed remediation unless logic is custom.

stem: An application has a long, resource-intensive instance initialization process, taking 15 or more minutes to warm caches, which makes standard scale-out events too slow to meet demand spikes. The team wants pre-initialized instances ready to be put into service almost immediately when scaling out, without keeping them fully in the live traffic pool and its associated compute cost while idle. Which Auto Scaling feature best fits this need?

choices.text: A longer health check grace period so instances have time to become healthy
Launch lifecycle hooks with a long Pending:Wait timeout on every scale-out
Scheduled scaling that scales out hours before anticipated demand
Auto Scaling warm pools

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Warm pools keep pre-initialized instances ready, so scale-out skips the 15-minute warm-up.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Longer grace period: doesn't speed readiness.
• Long lifecycle hooks: still wait each time.
• Scheduled scale-out hours early: wasteful and misses surprises.

Key takeaway: long initialization → warm pools.

stem: Security needs one queryable view of Config compliance across 40 accounts and 3 Regions, including SQL-style advanced queries. Which solution fits?

choices.text: Athena queries against each account's Config delivery bucket
Cross-account roles assumed on demand to call Config APIs
One Config rule deployed manually to each account and Region
An organization Config aggregator, with advanced queries

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An aggregator collects configuration and compliance data from all accounts and Regions, and Config advanced queries run SQL-like queries across the aggregated data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Athena on delivery buckets: possible but requires building and maintaining the pipeline.
• Manual rules: deploy rules, not a unified view.
• Assuming roles on demand: slow and manual.

Key takeaway: organization-wide Config view → aggregator + advanced query.

stem: A Config rule flags non-compliant S3 buckets that lack default encryption, and an automatic remediation action using an SSM Automation document has been attached. Compliance status correctly changes to NON_COMPLIANT, but the remediation action never executes, and the Config console shows no remediation execution history at all. What is the most likely root cause?

choices.text: Automatic remediation requires clicking Remediate in the console each time.
The remediation role can't be assumed by SSM or lacks S3 encryption permissions.
The bucket is in a different Region than the Config rule, which is never supported.
AWS Config remediation supports only EC2 and IAM resources, not S3 buckets.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Automatic remediation fails if SSM can't assume the remediation role or the role lacks s3:PutEncryptionConfiguration.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Requires clicking: automatic remediation doesn't.
• Different Region: Config rules are Regional but that's not the issue.
• S3 unsupported: S3 is supported.

Key takeaway: remediation needs a working role with permissions.

stem: A team is building a remediation action that must run for up to 45 minutes to safely drain and replace a fleet of stateful instances, using AWS-provided logic where possible to reduce custom code. Which factor most strongly favors using an SSM Automation runbook over a Lambda function for this specific remediation?

choices.text: Automation runbooks aren't bound by Lambda's 15-minute limit and many are prebuilt.
Lambda functions cannot be triggered by AWS Config remediation actions at all.
SSM Automation runbooks run free of charge, while Lambda always incurs cost.
SSM documents can only be written in Python, which the team already uses.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SSM Automation runbooks aren't bound by Lambda's 15-minute limit and include many built-in actions for long operations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lambda can't be triggered by Config: it can.
• SSM free vs. Lambda: not the key reason.
• Python only: SSM supports multiple step types.

Key takeaway: long remediation → Automation runbooks.

stem: After deploying a new AMI to an Auto Scaling group's launch template, the operations team expected all running instances to be gradually replaced with the new AMI version, but a week later most instances are still running the old AMI, only being replaced individually as they fail health checks. What should the team do to proactively roll out the new AMI to the entire fleet in a controlled way?

choices.text: Start an instance refresh
Wait for normal scaling and health replacements
Update the launch template version again
Terminate all instances at once and let them relaunch

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An instance refresh replaces running instances gradually with ones launched from the updated template, respecting minimum healthy percentage.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Wait for natural replacement: may never happen.
• Update the template again: doesn't replace instances.
• Terminate all at once: downtime.

Key takeaway: roll out new AMIs → instance refresh.

stem: A rule must evaluate S3 bucket public access immediately whenever a bucket policy changes, and also re-check all buckets daily in case a change was missed. Which trigger configuration fits?

choices.text: Both change and periodic triggers
Manual trigger run by an administrator daily
Periodic trigger at the minimum interval only
Configuration change trigger only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Config rules can use a configuration change trigger (evaluates when a recorded resource changes) and a periodic trigger (evaluates on a schedule). Using both gives immediate detection plus a daily safety net.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Periodic only: delays detection.
• Change only: misses cases where recording didn't capture a change.
• Manual: not automatic.

Key takeaway: change triggers for immediacy, periodic for completeness.

stem: An operations engineer needs a cross-account view of patch compliance for thousands of instances and the ability to open a session or browse file systems on a noncompliant instance from the same console. Which capability fits?

choices.text: AWS Config conformance packs
Change Manager requests
Parameter Store hierarchies
Patch Manager compliance plus Fleet Manager

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Patch Manager reports compliance, and Fleet Manager provides a unified console to view managed nodes and perform actions such as sessions, file system browsing, and performance views.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Change Manager: approvals for changes, not fleet operations.
• Parameter Store: configuration values.
• Conformance packs: compliance rules, with no instance management.

Key takeaway: fleet visibility and actions → Fleet Manager.

stem: During an incident, the team must find the top error messages across 60 log streams in one log group over 2 hours and see how their counts changed every 5 minutes. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Create a metric filter and wait for new data to accumulate
Open each stream in the console and read chronologically
Logs Insights: filter errors, stats by message and bin(5m)
Download all streams and grep them locally

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Logs Insights queries across all streams in a log group for any time range, with filter, stats, and bin() for time-bucketed counts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Metric filter: applies only to new data, not the past 2 hours.
• Local grep: slow and manual.
• Reading streams: impractical at this scale.

Key takeaway: ad hoc aggregation over historical logs → Logs Insights.

stem: A CodeDeploy blue/green deployment to an ECS service was configured with CloudWatch alarm-based automatic rollback, referencing an alarm on the target group's 5XX error count metric. During a recent bad deployment, error rates spiked dramatically, but the deployment completed successfully without rolling back, and the alarm remained in the OK state throughout. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: Alarm-based rollback works only for Lambda deployments, not ECS deployments.
The alarm's evaluation settings were longer than the bake time.
The rollback failed because the deployment was in-place rather than blue/green.
CodeDeploy supports alarm-based rollback only for EC2 and on-premises deployments.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
If the alarm's evaluation window is longer than the deployment bake time, the deployment completes before the alarm can fire, so no rollback occurs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lambda-only rollback: ECS supports it.
• In-place vs. blue/green: not the cause.
• EC2 only: ECS supports alarms.

Key takeaway: alarm windows must fit within bake time.

stem: A pipeline's CodeBuild action shows only 'Build failed'. The engineer must find the failing command and also keep logs for 90 days for audits. What should the engineer check and configure?

choices.text: The CodePipeline execution summary, which contains full build output
The artifact bucket, which stores an error file
CodeBuild logs, with 90-day retention
CloudTrail event history, which records compiler errors

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeBuild streams build output to CloudWatch Logs (and optionally S3). Setting log group retention or S3 lifecycle meets the audit period.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Pipeline summary: shows action status only.
• CloudTrail: records API calls, not command output.
• Artifact bucket: stores artifacts, not logs.

Key takeaway: build output lives in CodeBuild logs; manage their retention.

stem: A DevOps team wants every CloudWatch alarm breach on production RDS instances to automatically generate a centralized, trackable operational work item with contextual details such as related resources and runbook links, so engineers can triage and assign it, rather than relying solely on ephemeral SNS email notifications. Which capability should they configure?

choices.text: Keep SNS email notifications.
Have the alarms create Systems Manager OpsCenter OpsItems.
Create a CloudTrail Insights rule that tracks alarm state transitions as tickets.
Use AWS Config to record alarm state changes as configuration items.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudWatch alarms can create OpsCenter OpsItems automatically, giving a centralized, trackable record of each breach.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SNS email: not tracked.
• CloudTrail Insights: API anomalies.
• Config items: configuration, not alarm events.

Key takeaway: trackable operational issues → OpsItems.

stem: A company's public-facing checkout API occasionally fails silently from certain external network paths in ways that internal health checks and server-side metrics do not catch, because the server continues to report healthy while the actual customer-facing request path through CloudFront and external DNS resolution breaks. Which monitoring approach would most directly detect this class of failure before customers report it?

choices.text: Increase the frequency of the ALB target group's internal health checks.
A CloudWatch Synthetics canary exercising the external checkout path.
Add granular custom metrics in the application tracking internal processing time.
Enable Container Insights on the ECS cluster that hosts the checkout service.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Synthetics canary exercising the external checkout path from outside detects failures that internal health checks can't see.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More frequent internal checks: still internal.
• Internal metrics: miss external path issues.
• Container Insights: resource metrics.

Key takeaway: external user experience → canaries.

stem: An ECS service running on Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer is stuck continuously cycling tasks: new tasks start, briefly register with the target group, then are deregistered and stopped shortly after, and the service never reaches a steady desired count. CloudWatch Logs show the application logging that the server started successfully on its port in each task. What should the engineer check next to diagnose the deregistration?

choices.text: The target group health check settings and that security groups allow the ALB.
Whether the task definition's CPU and memory are set to the maximum allowed values.
Whether the ECS cluster has Container Insights enabled for the service.
Whether the Fargate platform version is set to LATEST for the service.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Tasks that pass container startup but fail the ALB check get replaced in a loop. Check the target group health check path and port, and that security groups allow the ALB to reach tasks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Max CPU/memory: not the cause.
• Container Insights: monitoring only.
• Platform version: unlikely.

Key takeaway: cycling tasks → health checks and SG paths.

stem: An engineer investigating a production incident finds that several pods in an EKS cluster are in a CrashLoopBackOff state. The engineer wants a consolidated view of container-level CPU and memory metrics correlated with pod restart counts and logs, without manually running commands against each node. Which AWS-native tool provides this consolidated operational view for EKS?

choices.text: Amazon Inspector container image scanning
AWS X-Ray traces for the affected services
AWS Config evaluation of the cluster's configuration
CloudWatch Container Insights

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Container Insights collects pod and container metrics and logs, including restarts, to diagnose CrashLoopBackOff.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Inspector: vulnerabilities.
• X-Ray: request traces.
• Config: configuration.

Key takeaway: container health → Container Insights.

stem: A platform team wants a single view that combines distributed trace data with the corresponding CloudWatch metrics and logs for each service in their microservices architecture, so they can pivot from a slow trace directly to the relevant service's dashboard and logs without switching consoles. Which capability provides this integrated experience, building on top of raw X-Ray trace data?

choices.text: AWS X-Ray alone, which already displays CloudWatch metrics and logs natively within its trace view without any additional configuration.
CloudWatch ServiceLens, which integrates X-Ray traces with CloudWatch metrics, logs, and alarms in a unified service map and view.
Amazon Detective, which is designed to correlate trace data for security investigations only.
AWS Config aggregator, which combines trace and metric data across accounts.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ServiceLens (now part of CloudWatch Application Signals) combines X-Ray traces with CloudWatch metrics and logs in one view.

Why the other options are wrong:
• X-Ray alone: limited integration.
• Detective: security investigations.
• Config aggregator: configuration.

Key takeaway: traces + metrics + logs together → ServiceLens.

stem: Several EC2 instances in a production Auto Scaling group unexpectedly began failing health checks and were replaced by the group. Reviewing AWS Health events for the account reveals a scheduled EC2 instance retirement event listing those exact instance IDs, issued due to underlying hardware degradation. What is the most appropriate root-cause conclusion and follow-up action?

choices.text: Hardware degradation per the Health event; verify impact and automate proactive replacement.
The Health event is unrelated, since Health reports only informational maintenance windows.
Open a support case disputing the retirement, since retirements are always customer misconfigurations.
No action is needed, since Auto Scaling replaced the instances automatically.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Health event about hardware degradation explains the failures. Verify the impact and automate responses (for example, EventBridge rules on Health events) for next time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Unrelated: it's the cause.
• Dispute retirements: not appropriate.
• No action: automate future handling.

Key takeaway: Health events explain infrastructure-driven failures.

stem: A production CloudFormation stack has been running stably for months, but the team suspects that an engineer manually modified a security group rule directly in the EC2 console during a recent incident, bypassing the stack. They want to confirm exactly which resources and properties have diverged from the stack's defined template before deciding whether to update the template or revert the manual change. What should they do?

choices.text: Delete and recreate the stack, since CloudFormation cannot detect out-of-band changes.
Run drift detection and review each resource's differing properties.
Compare the template line by line against each resource's current console settings.
Enable AWS Config recording.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Drift detection compares current resource configurations with the template and shows differing properties.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Can't detect: it can.
• Manual comparison: slow.
• Config alone: doesn't compare with the template.

Key takeaway: manual changes to stacks → drift detection.

stem: A company's central security team created an IAM role in a shared services account that third-party auditors assume via STS AssumeRole to review logs. The team wants to prevent the confused deputy problem where the third party's own AWS account could be tricked by an attacker into assuming the role. Which control should be added to the role's trust policy?

choices.text: Restrict the trust policy to a source IP range with aws:SourceIp
Attach a permissions boundary limiting the role's maximum permissions
Require a unique ExternalId in the trust policy
Require MFA with aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent in the trust policy

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Requiring a unique ExternalId in the trust policy prevents the confused deputy problem when third parties assume the role.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Source IP: fragile.
• Permissions boundary: limits permissions, not who can assume.
• MFA: third-party automated assumption may not use MFA.

Key takeaway: third-party roles → ExternalId.

stem: An account in an OU has an SCP that explicitly denies ec2:TerminateInstances, but a developer in that account still successfully terminates an EC2 instance. The IAM policy simulator shows the developer's identity policy allows the action, and no other SCP in the OU hierarchy grants it. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: An explicit Allow in the developer's identity policy overrides the SCP's Deny
SCPs affect only the root user, not IAM roles in the account
It's the management account, which SCPs don't affect
The SCP was attached to the wrong OU and does not apply to this account

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SCPs don't affect the management account. If the developer is in the management account, the deny doesn't apply.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Allow overrides SCP: false.
• SCPs only affect root: false.
• Wrong OU: possible, but the telling case is the management account.

Key takeaway: SCPs never restrict the management account.

stem: An IAM policy denies all actions unless aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is true, intended to force MFA for all API calls. After deployment, automated CI/CD pipelines using an IAM role begin failing all AWS API calls. What is the root cause?

choices.text: Roles assumed via AssumeRole cannot use MFA-conditioned policies at all
The policy needs an explicit Allow statement in addition to the Deny
CI/CD pipelines must use IAM users instead of roles for MFA to work
Non-MFA role sessions lack the MFA key, so the Deny applies

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Role sessions from AssumeRole without MFA don't carry aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent, so a Deny-unless-MFA policy blocks CI/CD roles. Use BoolIfExists or exclude those roles.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Roles can't use MFA conditions: they can.
• Need an explicit Allow: the Deny still applies.
• Must use IAM users: no.

Key takeaway: MFA conditions and role sessions need care.

stem: A team runs workloads on Amazon EKS and wants pods to obtain temporary AWS credentials scoped to least-privilege IAM roles per pod, without storing long-term credentials in container images or Kubernetes secrets. Which mechanism should they implement?

choices.text: Store and rotate static IAM credentials for each pod in Secrets Manager
Store IAM access keys in a Kubernetes Secret mounted into each pod
Use the worker node instance profile role shared across all pods
IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IRSA (or EKS Pod Identity) gives each service account its own IAM role and temporary credentials.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Static credentials in Secrets Manager: long-term keys.
• Keys in Kubernetes Secrets: long-term keys.
• Node role for all pods: not least privilege.

Key takeaway: per-pod IAM → IRSA / Pod Identity.

stem: An application in Account B needs to retrieve a secret stored in Secrets Manager in Account A, which is encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key in Account A. What must be configured, at minimum, for the cross-account retrieval to succeed?

choices.text: Only the KMS key policy needs to allow Account B; the Secrets Manager resource policy is optional
Only a Secrets Manager resource policy granting Account B's role secretsmanager:GetSecretValue; KMS permissions are not involved
Account B must copy the KMS key into its own account first
Both a Secrets Manager resource policy granting Account B's role access, and the KMS key policy granting that role kms:Decrypt

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-account secrets need a Secrets Manager resource policy granting Account B's role, and a KMS key policy allowing it to decrypt (plus B's identity policy).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Key policy only: secret policy needed too.
• Secret policy only: key access needed too.
• Copy the key: not possible.

Key takeaway: cross-account secret = secret policy + key policy.

stem: An admin updates the DataAnalyst permission set in IAM Identity Center. Users in 12 accounts still have old permissions. What explains this, and what fixes it?

choices.text: Reprovision the permission set to the accounts
Permission sets apply only to new users; recreate the users
Identity Center caches policies in the browser; clear cookies
Changes take 24 hours to propagate automatically

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Identity Center creates an IAM role (AWSReservedSSO_...) in each assigned account from the permission set. After editing a permission set, it must be provisioned to the assigned accounts so those roles are updated.

Why the other options are wrong:
• New users only: assignments aren't user-creation dependent.
• 24-hour propagation: there's no such automatic delay; provisioning pushes changes.
• Browser cache: permissions are evaluated by IAM on the role, not the browser.

Key takeaway: permission set → IAM role per account; reprovision after changes.

stem: A Lambda function in Account 111111111111 attempts sts:AssumeRole into a role in Account 222222222222 and receives AccessDenied. The target role's trust policy Principal correctly lists the Lambda execution role's ARN, and the code uses the correct target role ARN. What is the most likely missing piece?

choices.text: The Lambda execution role also needs an Allow for sts:AssumeRole on the target role
STS is a global service and does not support cross-account AssumeRole calls from Lambda
Lambda functions cannot assume roles in other accounts, only roles in their own account
The target role needs a resource-based policy in addition to its trust policy to be assumed

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-account AssumeRole needs both the target role's trust policy and an Allow for sts:AssumeRole on that role ARN in the caller's (Lambda execution role's) policy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• STS doesn't support cross-account: it does.
• Lambda can't assume other accounts' roles: it can.
• Resource-based policy beyond trust: the trust policy is the role's resource policy.

Key takeaway: AssumeRole needs trust on the target and permission on the caller.

stem: A custom rotation Lambda for a third-party API key must never leave applications with an invalid key during rotation. Which step order does Secrets Manager call, and where is the new key activated in the vendor system?

choices.text: createSecret, testSecret, setSecret, finishSecret; activate in testSecret
finishSecret first to stage AWSPENDING, then the other steps
setSecret, createSecret, finishSecret, testSecret; activate in finishSecret
createSecret, setSecret, testSecret, finishSecret; activate in setSecret

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Rotation runs createSecret (generate the new value as AWSPENDING), setSecret (apply it in the target system), testSecret (verify it works), and finishSecret (move AWSCURRENT to the new version). Apps keep using AWSCURRENT until finishSecret, so they're never left with an unusable key.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Other orders: CreateSecret must come first and finishSecret last.
• finishSecret first: would promote a value before it exists or is tested.

Key takeaway: create → set → test → finish; staging labels keep clients safe.

stem: An Organizations administrator wants a preventive control restricting which external principals can be granted access through resource-based policies on resources within a specific OU (for example, limiting which accounts an S3 bucket policy or KMS key policy may name as a principal), complementing existing SCPs which govern principal permissions. Which feature is designed for this?

choices.text: Tag policies enforcing consistent resource tagging
Declarative policies for account-level settings
Resource control policies (RCPs)
Service control policies (SCPs) on the principals

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Resource control policies (RCPs) set org-wide limits on who can access resources, such as blocking external principals.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Tag policies: tags.
• Declarative policies: account settings.
• SCPs: limit principals, not resources.

Key takeaway: restrict external access to resources → RCPs.

stem: An application behind Amazon CloudFront experiences an HTTP flood from many distinct IP addresses at a rate that individually stays under typical thresholds but collectively overwhelms the origin, alongside occasional large-scale network-layer volumetric spikes. Which combination of controls addresses both threats appropriately?

choices.text: AWS Shield Advanced alone, since it replaces the need for WAF rules
WAF rate-based rules for L7 plus Shield Advanced for L3/L4 and cost protection
AWS WAF rate-based rules alone, which handle both layer 3/4 and layer 7 attacks
Strict inbound security group rules, which mitigate both types of attack

explanation:
Why this is correct:
WAF rate-based rules can aggregate on keys other than IP (for example, headers) to catch distributed L7 floods, and Shield Advanced adds L3/L4 protection and cost protection.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shield Advanced alone: needs WAF for L7 rules.
• WAF alone: not L3/L4.
• Security groups: not DDoS mitigation.

Key takeaway: L7 floods → WAF; L3/L4 → Shield Advanced.

stem: An SG allows TCP 443 from 203.0.113.0/24, but connections still fail. The subnet NACL has rule 90 DENY 203.0.113.0/24 all traffic and rule 100 ALLOW 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. What is happening?

choices.text: Security groups override NACLs, so the SG allow should win
The NACL's rule 90 matches first and denies the traffic
NACL rules apply only to outbound traffic
NACLs evaluate the most specific rule regardless of number

explanation:
Why this is correct:
NACLs evaluate rules in ascending number order and stop at the first match, so rule 90's DENY wins before rule 100 is considered. Both NACL and SG must allow traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SG overrides: both layers must allow.
• Most specific wins: NACLs use rule order, not specificity.
• Outbound only: NACLs have inbound and outbound rules.

Key takeaway: NACL = first match by rule number.

stem: A company has a multi-VPC architecture using a centralized inspection VPC and Transit Gateway, and needs to enforce domain-based egress filtering (allow only specific outbound FQDNs) for all spoke VPCs, with centrally managed rules. Which service should be deployed in the inspection VPC?

choices.text: Security groups applied in each spoke VPC with domain rules
VPC Flow Logs with an automated Lambda remediation function
Network Firewall domain-list rules via Transit Gateway
AWS WAF attached to an Application Load Balancer in each spoke

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS Network Firewall in the inspection VPC with domain-list rules enforces domain filtering for all traffic routed through the Transit Gateway.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Security groups: no domain rules.
• Flow Logs remediation: reactive.
• WAF on ALBs: inbound HTTP only.

Key takeaway: central egress domain filtering → Network Firewall.

stem: A Control Tower administrator enables a guardrail that uses an SCP to block disabling CloudTrail in member accounts, and separately enables a guardrail that uses an AWS Config rule to flag accounts where CloudTrail is disabled. How should these two guardrail types be characterized?

choices.text: Both are preventive guardrails
The SCP guardrail is preventive; the Config rule guardrail is detective
The SCP guardrail is detective, and the Config rule guardrail is preventive
Both are detective, because Control Tower supports only detective guardrails

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SCP-based guardrails prevent actions. Config rule-based guardrails detect and report noncompliance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Both preventive: Config rules detect.
• Reversed: incorrect.
• Both detective: SCPs are preventive.

Key takeaway: preventive = SCP; detective = Config.

stem: Customer export files land in an S3 bucket daily. The company wants alerts within minutes when a file contains card numbers, and wants the finding to trigger automatic quarantine of the object. Which design fits?

choices.text: Config rules that check bucket encryption
Macie jobs; findings via EventBridge to Lambda
Inspector scans of the bucket with automated remediation
GuardDuty S3 Protection findings that trigger quarantine

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Macie classification jobs scoped to new objects detect card numbers, and Macie findings are published to EventBridge, where a rule can invoke Lambda to move or tag the object.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GuardDuty S3 Protection: detects suspicious access, not data content.
• Config encryption rules: encryption status, not content.
• Inspector: vulnerabilities, not data classification.

Key takeaway: content-based alerts on S3 data → Macie findings + EventBridge.

stem: A financial services company must use FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated hardware for cryptographic key storage and requires direct control over the HSM, including using PKCS#11, JCE, or CNG APIs directly against it, which rules out standard AWS KMS. What should they deploy, and how can it still integrate with KMS-based services if needed?

choices.text: AWS CloudHSM, optionally as a KMS custom key store
S3 server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C) instead of HSMs
Secrets Manager with an HSM-backed KMS key, which is identical to CloudHSM
Standard KMS customer managed keys

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudHSM provides FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated, single-tenant HSMs, and can back a KMS custom key store.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SSE-C: key management shifts to you, not an HSM.
• Secrets Manager identical to CloudHSM: false.
• Standard KMS keys: not dedicated HSMs you control.

Key takeaway: dedicated validated HSMs → CloudHSM.

stem: A security audit finds that dozens of EC2 instances have security groups allowing inbound SSH from 0.0.0.0/0 for administrative access. The DevOps team wants to eliminate inbound SSH exposure entirely while retaining shell access for troubleshooting. What is the recommended solution?

choices.text: A bastion host in a public subnet with the same security group rules
AWS Site-to-Site VPN used solely for SSH access
Systems Manager Session Manager (no inbound ports)
Restrict the SSH rule to the office's static IP range

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Session Manager provides shell access without inbound ports or SSH keys, with IAM control and logging.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bastion with the same rules: still exposed.
• VPN for SSH: still keys and ports.
• Office IP restriction: still SSH and keys.

Key takeaway: remove SSH exposure → Session Manager.

stem: During a large DDoS, an ALB-backed service scaled out for hours and the bill spiked. Which Shield Advanced benefit addresses this, and what is required?

choices.text: Discounts on Reserved Instances bought during attacks
Cost protection credits for protected resources
Automatic refunds for downtime on any resource
Free usage of all services during attacks

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Shield Advanced's DDoS cost protection provides credits for scaling charges on protected resources caused by attacks. The resource must be added to Shield Advanced protections.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Downtime refunds: not part of Shield.
• RI discounts and free usage: not offered.

Key takeaway: cost protection applies only to resources you protect.

stem: A security team wants to automatically scan EBS volumes attached to EC2 instances for malware whenever GuardDuty detects suspicious behavior on that instance, without deploying and managing third-party antivirus agents on every host. Which GuardDuty capability should they enable?

choices.text: GuardDuty Lambda Protection
GuardDuty S3 Protection
GuardDuty RDS Protection
GuardDuty Malware Protection for EC2

explanation:
Why this is correct:
GuardDuty Malware Protection for EC2 scans EBS volumes when suspicious activity is detected.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lambda Protection: Lambda network activity.
• S3 Protection: S3 access.
• RDS Protection: database logins.

Key takeaway: scan EC2 volumes for malware → Malware Protection for EC2.

stem: After GuardDuty raises a finding indicating a potentially compromised EC2 instance communicating with a known malicious IP, the security team wants to visualize related API calls, network traffic, and role assumptions over the preceding weeks to understand the full scope of the incident, without manually correlating raw CloudTrail and VPC Flow Logs. Which service is designed for this?

choices.text: AWS Trusted Advisor
AWS Config
Amazon Detective
Amazon Macie

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Detective builds behavior graphs from logs and findings to investigate what the instance did and with whom.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trusted Advisor: best practices.
• Config: configuration.
• Macie: sensitive data.

Key takeaway: investigate findings → Detective.

stem: A team creates an AWS WAF web ACL intending to protect an Application Load Balancer in us-east-1, but after association the rules do not take effect. Investigation shows the web ACL was created with scope CLOUDFRONT in us-east-1 instead of REGIONAL. What is the fix?

choices.text: Move the ALB to a Region that supports CLOUDFRONT-scoped web ACLs
Recreate the web ACL with REGIONAL scope in the ALB's Region
Nothing; WAF scope doesn't matter
Enable AWS Firewall Manager to bridge the scopes automatically

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ALBs need a REGIONAL web ACL in the ALB's Region. Recreate the web ACL with REGIONAL scope and associate it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Move the ALB: not how scopes work.
• Scope doesn't matter: it does.
• Firewall Manager bridging: doesn't change scope rules.

Key takeaway: ALB → REGIONAL web ACL.

stem: A compliance team enables automatic annual key rotation on a KMS key and expects it to also apply identically to a second KMS key created by importing external key material, as well as to a multi-Region primary key's replicas. Which statement accurately describes actual behavior?

choices.text: Imported key material can't auto-rotate; multi-Region keys rotate via the primary.
Automatic rotation applies to asymmetric keys the same way as symmetric keys.
Multi-Region KMS keys never support any form of rotation.
Rotation works identically for all key types, including imported material.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Keys with imported key material can't use automatic rotation, and multi-Region keys rotate from the primary. Rotation behavior differs by key type.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Asymmetric keys rotate the same: they don't support automatic rotation.
• Multi-Region never rotates: they do via the primary.
• Identical for all: not true.

Key takeaway: rotation depends on key type and origin.

stem: An auditor needs proof that CloudTrail logs in S3 were not altered or deleted after delivery, and proof that nobody can delete them for 7 years. Which combination fits?

choices.text: CloudTrail Lake plus a bucket policy denying deletes
CloudTrail Insights plus S3 Versioning
Config history plus MFA Delete
Log file validation plus Object Lock

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Log file integrity validation uses signed digest files to prove files weren't changed or removed. Object Lock in compliance mode prevents deletion for the retention period, even by root.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Insights and Versioning: Insights detects anomalies; versions can be deleted.
• Config and MFA Delete: Config doesn't verify log integrity; MFA Delete can be disabled by the owner.
• Bucket policy: administrators can change it.

Key takeaway: prove integrity → validation; enforce retention → Object Lock.

stem: A company wants any S3 bucket found without default encryption enabled to be automatically remediated within minutes, without human intervention, while keeping a record of what was changed and when. What should be configured?

choices.text: A CloudWatch alarm that emails the team when a bucket lacks encryption
An IAM policy that denies s3:PutObject on unencrypted buckets
An AWS CLI script run manually each week by an engineer
Config S3 encryption rule with SSM auto-remediation

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Config rule for S3 default encryption with SSM auto-remediation fixes buckets within minutes, across accounts if deployed org-wide.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Alarm emails: manual.
• IAM deny on PutObject: blocks usage, doesn't fix.
• Weekly script: slow.

Key takeaway: auto-fix bucket settings → Config + remediation.

stem: An engineer investigating a connectivity issue reviews VPC Flow Logs and sees REJECT entries for traffic from an application server to a database instance on port 3306, even though the security groups on both sides appear to permit the traffic. What should the engineer check next?

choices.text: Whether CloudTrail logged the calls that created the security groups
Whether the subnet's network ACL is rejecting the traffic
Whether the flow log format includes the pkt-srcaddr field
Whether GuardDuty has suppressed a related finding

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Flow log REJECT entries with permissive security groups point to the network ACL, which is stateless and may block traffic or return ports.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail: doesn't show traffic decisions.
• pkt-srcaddr: NAT visibility, not rejection cause.
• GuardDuty suppression: unrelated.

Key takeaway: REJECTs with open SGs → check NACLs.

stem: A team runs CloudFormation drift detection on a stack and it reports IN_SYNC for a security group resource, yet a manual console review shows an inbound rule was added outside CloudFormation. Which limitation of drift detection best explains this discrepancy?

choices.text: The stack must be in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE state for drift to be detected
Drift detection does not support security group resources at all
Drift detection runs automatically only every 24 hours, so it hasn't run yet
Drift detection has known gaps for some resources and list properties

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Drift detection doesn't detect every change (for example, some properties or resources, and changes to list properties not in the template). Review supported resources and properties.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rollback state needed: no.
• SGs unsupported: they're supported, with property caveats.
• 24-hour automatic run: drift detection is on demand.

Key takeaway: drift detection has known gaps.

stem: The team wants a page within 5 minutes when more than 10 AccessDenied errors occur from any single IAM principal in CloudTrail logs delivered to CloudWatch Logs. Which approach fits?

choices.text: AWS Config rules scanning CloudTrail content
A metric filter with principal as a dimension, and an alarm
GuardDuty, which has a built-in finding for this exact threshold
A daily Athena query over the S3 trail

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Metric filters can extract fields such as the principal ARN as dimensions, producing a metric per principal, and an alarm on that metric can page within minutes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GuardDuty: detects threats with its own logic, not custom thresholds.
• Daily Athena: too slow.
• Config: evaluates resource configuration, not log content.

Key takeaway: custom thresholds on log events → metric filter (with dimensions) + alarm.

stem: A security architect must choose the right tool for two scenarios: an IAM user's credentials being used from an unusual geographic location with reconnaissance-like API call patterns, and an S3 bucket's public access block setting being manually disabled, deviating from the required baseline. Which pairing is correct?

choices.text: Macie for anomalous behavior and GuardDuty for configuration drift
GuardDuty for both, since it also tracks configuration compliance
AWS Config for both, since it evaluates all account activity
GuardDuty for behavior; AWS Config rule for drift

explanation:
Why this is correct:
GuardDuty detects anomalous behavior, such as credentials used from unusual locations. A Config rule detects configuration drift from standards.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Macie/GuardDuty swapped: incorrect.
• GuardDuty for both: doesn't do configuration compliance.
• Config for both: doesn't detect behavior.

Key takeaway: behavior → GuardDuty; configuration → Config.

stem: A company's CloudTrail management events suddenly show a 20x spike in ec2:RunInstances calls from a single IAM role compared to the account's normal baseline, potentially indicating compromised credentials used for cryptomining. Which CloudTrail feature is designed to automatically surface this kind of anomaly without custom metric filters?

choices.text: CloudTrail log file integrity validation
CloudTrail Insights
CloudTrail data events for S3
An AWS Config resource timeline

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudTrail Insights detects unusual spikes in management API call volume, such as a 20× jump in RunInstances.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Integrity validation: tampering.
• S3 data events: object calls.
• Config timeline: configuration.

Key takeaway: API volume anomalies → CloudTrail Insights.

stem: An investigation into an S3 data exfiltration incident finds that CloudTrail management events show who accessed the bucket's configuration, but there is no record of the actual GetObject calls showing which objects were downloaded. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: CloudTrail never logs S3 activity under any configuration
GetObject calls are visible only in VPC Flow Logs, not CloudTrail
The bucket needs versioning enabled for GetObject calls to be logged
S3 object calls are data events, which must be enabled on the trail

explanation:
Why this is correct:
GetObject calls are data events and must be enabled on the trail to be logged.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Never logs S3: data events do.
• Only Flow Logs: incorrect.
• Versioning needed: no.

Key takeaway: object access auditing → data events.

stem: A company wants near-real-time streaming of CloudWatch Logs from application log groups in 30 member accounts into a centralized security account for correlation with a SIEM tool, rather than periodic batch exports. Which architecture is appropriate?

choices.text: A daily CreateExportTask from each log group to a bucket in the security account
Enable VPC Flow Logs in each account instead of application logs
Cross-account subscription filters to a central Kinesis stream
Copy log files manually with the CLI once per week

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-account subscription filters stream member accounts' logs into a central Kinesis stream in near real time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Daily exports: not near real time.
• Flow Logs instead: different data.
• Weekly CLI copies: manual.

Key takeaway: central real-time logs → cross-account subscriptions.

stem: A team deploys a payment Lambda function through CodeDeploy. It wants to send 10% of traffic to the new version for 5 minutes, then shift all traffic, and roll back automatically if the error-rate alarm fires during the deployment. Which configuration meets this?

choices.text: LambdaLinear10PercentEvery1Minute, without alarms on the deployment group.
LambdaAllAtOnce with a post-deployment validation test.
LambdaCanary10Percent5Minutes with the alarm and auto rollback.
A Lambda alias with a 10% routing weight updated manually after 5 minutes.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
LambdaCanary10Percent5Minutes sends 10% for 5 minutes, and an alarm on the deployment group rolls back automatically if errors rise.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Linear without alarms: no rollback.
• AllAtOnce: no gradual exposure.
• Manual alias weights: no automatic rollback.

Key takeaway: canary + alarms for safe Lambda releases.

stem: A CodePipeline in a tools account must deploy CloudFormation stacks into a production account. Artifacts are stored in an S3 bucket encrypted with a KMS customer managed key in the tools account. Which TWO configurations are required? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: A production-account role trusted by the tools account, assumed by the deploy action.
Duplicate the pipeline in the production account and run it there instead.
A key policy (and bucket policy) letting the production role decrypt the artifacts.
A VPC peering connection between the tools and production accounts.
The default AWS managed key aws/s3 for the artifact bucket, shared with production.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The pipeline assumes a role in the production account (trusted by the tools account), and the artifact bucket's KMS key policy (and bucket policy) lets that role decrypt artifacts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Duplicate pipelines: drift.
• VPC peering: not needed.
• aws/s3 managed key: can't be shared cross-account.

Key takeaway: cross-account pipelines = assumed role + KMS/bucket access.

stem: Developers and CodeBuild jobs download npm packages directly from the public registry. Security wants a central cache, the ability to block specific package versions, and continued builds if the public registry is briefly unavailable. Which solution fits BEST?

choices.text: An ECR repository that stores the npm packages as OCI artifacts.
CodeArtifact with an external connection to npmjs.
An S3 bucket where developers upload package tarballs manually.
A CodeBuild local cache for the node_modules directory.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeArtifact with an external connection to npmjs caches packages centrally and lets security control what's used.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ECR OCI artifacts: not an npm registry.
• Manual S3 uploads: toil.
• Local CodeBuild cache: per project, no governance.

Key takeaway: central package caching → CodeArtifact.

stem: CodeBuild builds for a Java project take 12 minutes, 8 of which are spent downloading Maven dependencies that rarely change. What is the MOST effective improvement?

choices.text: Use a larger EBS volume for the build container.
Increase the compute type to the largest available size.
Split the build into 10 parallel pipelines.
Cache the Maven repository directory in the project.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Caching the Maven local repository (for example, ~/.m2) between builds avoids re-downloading dependencies.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bigger EBS: not the bottleneck.
• Bigger compute: download time remains.
• Parallel pipelines: doesn't reduce downloads.

Key takeaway: repeated dependency downloads → build cache.

stem: A company must deploy a baseline stack (Config recorder, IAM roles, and alarms) into every existing account in an OU and automatically into any new account moved into that OU. Which approach requires the least ongoing effort?

choices.text: A StackSet with self-managed permissions, adding each new account ID manually.
A Lambda function that runs daily and creates stacks in all accounts.
A service-managed StackSet on the OU with automatic deployment.
Document the stack and ask each account owner to deploy it.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A service-managed StackSet targeting the OU with automatic deployment covers existing and future accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Self-managed with manual IDs: toil.
• Daily Lambda: reinvents StackSets.
• Account owners deploy: inconsistent.

Key takeaway: OU-wide baselines → service-managed StackSets.

stem: A stack update changes a property of an RDS DB instance that requires replacement. The team must never lose data if this happens by mistake and wants to see the impact before executing. What should it do?

choices.text: Enable drift detection on the stack before running the update.
UpdateReplacePolicy/DeletionPolicy Snapshot or Retain, and review a change set.
Set DeletionPolicy only, then run the update directly.
Enable termination protection on the stack before updating.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
UpdateReplacePolicy and DeletionPolicy set to Snapshot or Retain protect data when a replacement happens, and reviewing a change set reveals the replacement before executing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Drift detection: doesn't protect data.
• DeletionPolicy only: doesn't cover replacement.
• Termination protection: prevents stack deletion, not replacement.

Key takeaway: replacement risk → UpdateReplacePolicy + change sets.

stem: Operators sometimes modify security groups created by CloudFormation directly in the console. The DevOps team wants to be alerted automatically when a stack's resources no longer match the template. Which solution fits BEST?

choices.text: The Config rule cloudformation-stack-drift-detection-check with notifications.
Enable stack termination protection on all stacks.
Apply a stack policy that denies updates to security groups.
Enable CloudTrail and search manually for console changes each week.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The cloudformation-stack-drift-detection-check Config rule periodically checks stacks for drift and can notify.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Termination protection: unrelated.
• Stack policy: doesn't stop console changes.
• Manual CloudTrail search: slow.

Key takeaway: continuous drift monitoring → Config drift rule.

stem: An ECS service on EC2 capacity in three Availability Zones has 6 tasks. After a deployment, all tasks were placed in one AZ, and an AZ outage took the service down. What should the team configure?

choices.text: A distinctInstance placement constraint only.
A binpack placement strategy on memory.
Spread on attribute:ecs.availability-zone.
A larger desired count with the random strategy.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A spread strategy on attribute:ecs.availability-zone places tasks evenly across AZs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• distinctInstance: different instances, possibly same AZ.
• binpack: concentrates tasks.
• Random with more tasks: no guarantee.

Key takeaway: AZ balance for ECS on EC2 → spread by AZ.

stem: Before an Auto Scaling group terminates an instance during scale-in, the application must finish in-flight jobs and upload local logs to S3, which can take up to 10 minutes. Which feature enables this?

choices.text: A termination policy of OldestInstance.
Instance scale-in protection on all instances.
Increasing the ALB deregistration delay to 10 minutes.
A termination lifecycle hook completed after upload.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A termination lifecycle hook pauses termination until the application finishes and uploads, then completes the hook.

Why the other options are wrong:
• OldestInstance policy: chooses which, not how.
• Scale-in protection: blocks termination entirely.
• Deregistration delay: only connection draining.

Key takeaway: graceful scale-in → termination lifecycle hooks.

stem: A company has 40 workload accounts. The operations team wants to view metrics, logs, and traces from all accounts in one monitoring account and build cross-account dashboards without copying data. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: CloudWatch cross-account observability (monitoring account as sink).
Export all logs to S3 nightly and query them with Athena.
Subscribe every log group to a Kinesis stream in the monitoring account.
Create IAM users for the operations team in every account.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudWatch cross-account observability links source accounts to a monitoring account for unified metrics, logs, and traces.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Nightly S3 + Athena: not live.
• Kinesis per log group: logs only.
• IAM users everywhere: not a unified view.

Key takeaway: multi-account observability → cross-account observability.

stem: A Lambda function must publish high-cardinality custom business metrics at thousands of invocations per second. Calling PutMetricData synchronously adds latency and causes throttling. Which approach is recommended?

choices.text: Emit the metrics with CloudWatch embedded metric format.
Increase the function's memory to speed up PutMetricData calls.
Record the values as X-Ray annotations and use them as metrics.
Write the metrics to DynamoDB and aggregate them hourly.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EMF writes metrics in structured logs, extracted asynchronously by CloudWatch, avoiding PutMetricData throttling and latency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More memory: still API limits.
• X-Ray annotations: not metrics.
• DynamoDB hourly: not real-time metrics.

Key takeaway: high-volume custom metrics → EMF.

stem: On-call engineers receive five separate pages whenever a database slows down, because CPU, latency, error-rate, queue-depth, and 5xx alarms all fire together. The team wants a single page only when latency and error rate are both in ALARM. What should it implement?

choices.text: Delete every alarm except the CPU alarm.
Use anomaly detection on the CPU metric only.
Increase the evaluation periods on every alarm.
A composite alarm (AND of latency and errors).

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A composite alarm pages only when the key symptoms (latency AND errors) are alarming, while other alarms can notify quietly.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Delete alarms: loses signals.
• CPU anomaly only: misses symptoms.
• More periods: delays without deduplicating.

Key takeaway: alert on symptoms with composite alarms.

stem: Whenever an EC2 instance in production enters the 'stopped' state unexpectedly, the team wants to capture diagnostics, start the instance again, and notify the channel automatically. Which design fits BEST?

choices.text: EventBridge on the state-change event starting an SSM Automation runbook.
An Auto Scaling group with a desired capacity of 0.
A CloudWatch dashboard reviewed by the on-call engineer.
A cron job on a bastion host polling describe-instances hourly.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An EventBridge rule on the EC2 state-change (stopped) event starts an SSM Automation runbook that collects diagnostics and acts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ASG desired 0: unrelated.
• Dashboard review: manual.
• Hourly polling: slow.

Key takeaway: event-driven diagnostics → EventBridge + SSM.

stem: A CodeDeploy in-place deployment to EC2 fails in the ApplicationStop lifecycle event because the previously deployed revision's stop script is broken. The new revision contains a fixed script. How can the team get the new revision deployed?

choices.text: Increase the ApplicationStop timeout in the new appspec.yml.
Delete the deployment group and recreate it.
Change the deployment configuration to CodeDeployDefault.AllAtOnce.
Redeploy ignoring ApplicationStop failures.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
